Narrative: Violence in the north continued unabated with the military sustaining its heaviest losses since jihadist militants began operating in the country in 2021. Amid surge in attacks targeting military in country’s north since early 2025, large number of al-Qaeda-affiliated Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM) militants 17 April launched coordinated assaults on two military posts in northern Alibori department – one near Koudou Waterfalls and the other at so-called point triple in border area between Benin, Burkina Faso, and Niger. JNIM immediately claimed responsibility, alleging that 70 soldiers were killed, and govt 23 April acknowledged unprecedented death toll of 54 soldiers. West African regional bloc ECOWAS next day condemned “barbaric” act.

The military government’s hold on power appeared increasingly fragile as it claimed to have foiled a plot to overthrow President Traoré, pointing to neighbouring Côte d’Ivoire as the base of operations; jihadist militants launched a spate of attacks. Military govt denounced alleged coup attempt. In televised address, Security Minister Mahamadou Sana 21 April said security services had foiled coup plot planned for 16 April, claiming masterminds were based in neighbouring Côte d’Ivoire; Ivorian govt few days later denied involvement. Earlier in month, authorities had arrested unknown number of military personnel including two officers for allegedly planning to destabilise govt. As of late April, situation remained extremely tense across country with several army officers 22 April reportedly failing to attend army command meeting and some military camps placed on high supervision. Meanwhile, thousands 30 April demonstrated in support of govt in capital Ouagadougou after President Capt. Traoré in April repeatedly denounced “Western interference” in country’s internal affairs. Jihadist groups stepped up attacks in several regions. In Boucle du Mouhoun region, al-Qaeda-affiliated Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM) carried out reprisal attacks following alleged killing of large number of Fulani civilians by army and allies in Solenzo city in March. Notably, JNIM 3-5 April launched several raids in Lanfiera area, reportedly killing dozens of civilians suspected of collaborating with military or recently enlisted as army auxiliaries (VDPs). JNIM 21 April simultaneously attacked and captured three army camps in Boucle du Mouhoun, East and North regions with reportedly dozens of soldiers and VDPs killed. In Sahel region, Islamic State Sahel Province 15 April attacked Timboulel village, killing 15 civilians. In other important developments. Govt 6 April recalled ambassador to Algeria in solidarity with Bamako after Algerian authorities struck Malian drone (see Algeria, Mali). FM Karamoko Jean Marie Traoré, together with counterparts from Mali and Niger, 28 April met with Morocco’s King Mohamed VI, reiterated support for Morocco’s initiative to give Sahel countries access to Atlantic Ocean. In televised address, PM Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo 28 April announced govt’s plan to expand state control over foreign-owned industrial mines to secure larger share of revenues from country’s natural resources.

Authorities continued to grapple with the humanitarian fallout from the conflict in the DR Congo and further harassed critics through police searches and arrests ahead of the June-August elections. Response to growing refugee influx from DRC suffered new strains. Authorities late March started clearing Rugombo site sheltering tens of thousands of refugees from DR Congo in Citiboke province, citing overcrowding and need for buffer zone near DRC border. UN refugee agency and authorities attempted to relocate refugees to other camps such as Musenyi in Rutana province, but many refused citing concerns of lack of aid and drinking water there, opting to return home or remain in Rugombo despite official ban. Meanwhile, UN refugee agency 25 April warned worsening funding crisis affecting international humanitarian aid organisations threatens critical assistance to Congolese refugees in Burundi and strains relations with host communities. State-sanctioned repression and intimidation continued. Intelligence agents 2 April allegedly abducted main opposition party Congrès National pour la Liberté (CNL) supporter in Bujumbura province; 7 April arrested CNL executive and Mukaza communal councillor in Bujumbura city, Edouard Nzambimana, without warrant, and later reportedly transferred him to Mpimba prison. Police 21 April arrested two radio journalists at Kinama market in Bujumbura, reportedly accusing them of insurrection, and released them later same day. Meanwhile, president of National Independent Commission for Human Rights, Sixte Vigny Nimuraba, 18 April fled country after police searched his home. Nimuraba’s detractors pointed to commission’s internal rifts and graft claims, while others said accusations against Nimuraba underscore rising pressure on dissenting voices ahead of legislative, senatorial and communal polls set for June-August. Fuel crisis continued to threaten electoral timeline. Opposition figures including CNL secretary general Léopold Hakizimana 11 April warned persistent fuel shortages could hinder campaign operations by preventing candidates from reaching remote areas and engaging all potential voters, urging electoral commission and govt to address issue ahead of polls.

The political climate continued to heat up ahead of the October presidential election; security operations against Anglophone separatists in the Bakassi Peninsula fuelled tensions with neighbouring Nigeria. President Biya continued election manoeuvres as opposition tried to unite. Biya 8 April appointed ruling party Central Committee member Monique Ndongo to Constitutional Council, which is in charge of announcing official election results and resolving election disputes. Opposition parties and civil society leaders denounced Ndongo’s appointment as definitive undermining of body’s independence few months away from presidential election set for Oct. Meanwhile, calls for unified opposition gained momentum. Notably, runner-up in 2018 presidential election, Cabral Libii, 14 April urged opposition to rally behind common program and single candidate to defeat Biya. Meanwhile, U.S. 7 April decided to revoke Temporary Protected Status for Cameroonian nationals, putting some 8,000 at risk of deportation. Fearing influx of anti-govt diaspora members ahead of election, Biya signalled reluctance to cooperate in receiving deportation flights. Amid Anglophone conflict, insecurity in Bakassi threatened relations with Nigeria. Violent clashes persisted between govt forces and pro-Ambazonia separatists in North West (NW) and South West (SW) regions. Notably, Anglophone separatist fighters 6 April killed two govt soldiers in NW regional capital Bamenda, and another in ambush on checkpoint in Big Ngwandi village, Meme division (SW). Military tribunal 16 April sentenced vocal Anglophone activist Abdulkarim Ali to life imprisonment for allegedly supporting secession. After setting up ad hoc investigation committee in March, Nigerian Senate in April began to probe alleged annexation by Cameroon of Nigeria’s mangrove islands and maritime territories in Mbo area of Akwa Ibom state, which shares border with Cameroon in Bakassi Peninsula. Cameroon has increased military activity in Bakassi since Cameroonian pro-Ambazonia separatists strengthened cooperation with Nigerian Biafra separatist groups in 2023. Islamist insurgency continued to cause havoc in Far North region. State-run media 15 April highlighted worsening humanitarian crisis in Far North, including overcrowding of Minawao refugee camp, arrival of additional refugees amid Boko Haram insurgency’s advances in Nigeria’s Borno state, and lack of relief aid. Meanwhile, soldiers 3 April ambushed fighters from JAS faction of Boko Haram between Mozogo and Moskota town, Mayo-Tsanaga division, killing five.

President Touadéra continued his political manoeuvring to support his anticipated re-election bid, as authorities signed a deal with rebels to stabilise rural areas ahead of the December presidential vote, and intercommunal tensions rose in the east. Touadéra made overtures to opposition amid power struggle within ruling party. President Touadéra 8 April granted former ruling party official and would-be presidential candidate Henri-Marie Dondra rare audience, reportedly offering to release Dondra’s two brothers – arrested in March in connection with alleged assassination plot – in exchange for his Unité républicaine party aligning with ruling party; move came as Touadéra’s special adviser Fidèle Gouandjika accused some ruling party officials of seeking to discredit Dondra, highlighting ongoing factional infighting. Meanwhile, main opposition coalition Republican Bloc for the Defence of the Constitution 4 April held its largest demonstration since 2022, with several thousand people protesting in capital Bangui against Touadéra’s possible candidacy in presidential vote set for Dec; however, ineligibility of several coalition leaders and its relatively limited mobilisation capacity make it unlikely to pose serious threat to ruling party. In apparent appeasement bid, govt 21 April proposed political dialogue with opposition coalition, which 23 April signalled openness to talks. Govt reached truce with armed groups ahead of elections. As part of efforts to improve security situation in rural areas ahead of polls, govt 19 April signed agreement with two predominantly Fulani armed groups, Union for Peace in the Central African Republic (UPC) and Return, Reclamation and Rehabilitation (3R); groups committed to reintegrating into peace process and immediately ceasing hostilities as part of deal, which may result in integration of rebel representatives into govt. Intercommunal tensions intensified in eastern region. Nearly 100 people, some of whom were armed, 4 April attempted to storm sub-prefect’s residence in Zemio town (Haut-Mbomou prefecture), with national army firing warning shots to disperse crowd. Protesters denounced arrest of ethnic Zande militia leader suspected of orchestrating late-March attack on humanitarian convoy, which left one NGO worker and three ethnic Fulani civilians dead near Zemio. Amid mounting tensions between Zande and Fulani communities since attack, Zande armed group 14 April abducted ten civilians near Mboki town (Haut-Mbomou), before releasing them next day.

Amid mounting tensions over N’Djamena’s involvement in the Sudanese conflict, President Déby consolidated his control over the military to deter a potential coup; the government reached a peace agreement with a self-defence militia in the country’s north. President Déby sacked several ethnic Zaghawa army officials. Under growing pressure from his Zaghawa ethnic group over Chad’s alleged support for Sudanese paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, Déby 11 April demoted Gen. Bahar Mahamat Itno – his cousin and former army chief of staff, who previously threatened to overthrow regime – to lowest military rank and dismissed him from army. Déby 14 April demoted and dismissed another nine senior Zaghawa military officers. Unprecedented sanctions appeared to serve as warning to Zaghawa elite that defiance would not be tolerated. Security force misconduct fuelled tensions with locals, 130 inmates escaped in jailbreak. Gendarmerie officer 13 April killed civilian in Zowar town (Tibesti province), sparking anger from locals who set gendarmerie post on fire. Nomadic Guard 14 April opened fire on residents of Bissi Mafou village (Mayo-Kebbi Ouest province) in unclear circumstances, leaving three dead. Meanwhile, over 130 prisoners 18 April escaped from jail in Mongo town (Guéra province); at least four dead in shootout. Govt signed peace deal with militia in gold-rich region. Govt 20 April reached peace agreement with Miski self-defence group (Tibesti province), created in 2018 amid mounting tensions over management of region’s gold wealth. Deal included general amnesty for members of security forces and militiamen involved in clashes, and suspension of all mining permits and activities until mapping studies are completed. Chad and Saudi Arabia deepened relations. Chadian and Saudi foreign ministers 12 April met in Türkiye in apparent follow-up to Déby’s talks with Saudi govt officials in March. Rapprochement could enable N’Djamena to secure funding and mitigate internal stability risks associated with Chadian combatants’ return from Sudan, by providing fighters to Riyadh amid speculation around U.S.-backed ground offensive against Houthis in Yemen (see Yemen and Saudi Arabia); Saudi Arabia, for its part, may be seeking to counter influence of its rival United Arab Emirates, which has used Chadian territory as key hub for supporting paramilitary forces in Sudan.

Political tensions surged as authorities barred the main opposition leader from contesting the October presidential election; meanwhile, Burkina Faso accused Côte d’Ivoire of harbouring the masterminds of a coup plot. Top opposition figure struck off electoral register. Court in Abidjan city 22 April ordered removal from electoral list of main opposition Democratic Party of Côte d’Ivoire leader and would-be presidential candidate Tidjane Thiam on grounds he no longer had Ivorian nationality. Decision, which cannot be appealed, is based on article 48 of Nationality Code stating that Ivorian adults lose citizenship if they voluntarily obtain another nationality; Thiam acquired French nationality in 1987, but renounced it in Feb to run in Oct presidential election, as candidates cannot hold dual citizenship. Thiam immediately rejected court’s decision, calling it “act of democratic vandalism”, and Democratic Party of Côte d’Ivoire 28 April said it had launched legal action to challenge Thiam’s exclusion, alleging procedural violations. Earlier, Thiam’s party and former President Gbagbo’s opposition African People’s Party-Côte d’Ivoire 11-12 April suspended their participation in electoral commission, denouncing its lack of independence and demanding “audit” of voters’ list. In media interview, head of Catholic Bishops’ Conference of Côte d’Ivoire 9 April also questioned “independence” of election body. With six months to go before polls, exclusion of candidates and electoral commission’s lack of credibility are raising prospect of electoral violence. Authorities arrested suspected jihadists from Mali and Burkina Faso. French newspaper Le Monde 18 April reported Ivorian intelligence services early Feb had partially dismantled network linked to al-Qaeda and comprising Malian and Burkinabè nationals in southern Côte d’Ivoire; article alleged network was seeking to recruit fighters to combat in Sahel region. Tensions with Ouagadougou spiked over alleged coup plot in Burkina Faso. In televised address, Burkina Faso Security Minister Mahamadou Sana 21 April said security services had foiled “major plot” to overthrow President Capt. Traoré, pointing to Côte d’Ivoire as base of operations (see Burkina Faso); Côte d’Ivoire govt spokesperson Amadou Coulibaly days later denied involvement. Ouagadougou had made similar allegations against Côte d’Ivoire in 2024 amid increasingly tense bilateral relations.

A diplomatic breakthrough could pave the way for de-escalation in the eastern DR Congo, as Kigali and Kinshasa committed to drafting a peace agreement by early May; meanwhile, authorities accused former President Kabila of treason. Kinshasa, Kigali and M23 rebels pledged to de-escalate conflict in eastern DRC. Congolese FM Thérèse Kayikwamba and Rwandan counterpart Olivier Nduhungirehe 25 April signed “declaration of principles” under U.S. auspices, committing to “immediate de-escalation” of conflict in eastern DRC and pledging to draft peace deal by 2 May. In parallel, Washington continued to negotiate minerals deals with both Kinshasa and Kigali. Meanwhile, direct talks between Congolese govt and Rwanda-backed M23 rebels 9 April kicked off in Doha, Qatar. Despite sticking points, parties 23 April signed joint declaration pledging to halt fighting and work toward permanent truce. M23 advance in North and South Kivu provinces stalled. M23 early April withdrew from strategic town of Walikale in North Kivu, describing move as goodwill gesture ahead of Doha talks. Withdrawal coincided with U.S. Senior Adviser for Africa Massad Boulos’s tour of Great Lakes region and M23’s increasing difficulties in maintaining control over recently-conquered areas, with emergence of “pockets of resistance” often claimed by pro-govt Wazalendo militias. Notably, in South Kivu, Wazalendo 13 April deployed in Kavumu and Kabamba towns (Kabare territory); however, Kavumu airport remained under M23 control and M23 rebels retook Kabamba by 15 April. Fighting between M23 and Wazalendo also reported in neighbouring Kalehe territory, notably 21-27 April. Meanwhile in North Kivu, M23 rebels 11-12 April clashed with govt and Wazalendo forces in provincial capital Goma; Interior Ministry 12 April blamed M23 for attack, said 52 people killed, but Wazalendo claimed responsibility, signalling mounting misalignment between army and allies. Southern African regional force 29 April began withdrawal of troops billeted in UN compounds since M23's Jan takeover of Goma. Kabila’s alleged return to DRC caused stir within govt. Amid rumour of former President Kabila’s visit to M23-controlled city of Goma, govt 18 April accused Kabila of high treason, ordering asset seizure, and Interior Ministry next day banned Kabila’s party, condemning its “ambiguous stance” on M23. Military court 30 April requested Senate lift Kabila’s immunity as lifetime senator to investigate alleged ties to M23’s political wing, Alliance Fleuve Congo.

A leadership change in Ethiopia’s Tigray region created a fragile opening to ease tensions between Asmara and Addis Ababa; Eritrea continued manoeuvring to influence regional dynamics in the Horn of Africa. Prospects for de-escalation between Asmara and Addis Ababa remained uncertain. After Ethiopian PM Abiy 8 April appointed Lt. Gen. Tadesse Werede as new Tigray interim president (see Ethiopia), tensions in Tigray momentarily eased, offering window for de-escalation between Ethiopia and Eritrea amid latter’s meddling in Tigray’s political dispute. Significant challenges persisted, however. Under pressure from federal govt, Tadesse agreed to eight-point pledge, including commitment to sever ties with both domestic and foreign actors not involved in negotiation of 2022 Pretoria Agreement, which ended Tigray war; Tadesse may lack authority or means to enforce clause, widely seen as directive for Tigray People’s Liberation Front to cut connections with Eritrea, which are managed directly by senior figures within Tigray’s security apparatus. Adding to challenges, Eritrea remained on military standby, with troops stationed in key border areas and all citizens under age of 60 barred from leaving country, keeping tensions elevated. Authorities maintained active diplomatic engagement on Sudan and South Sudan. Asmara continued to support Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) in their war against paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). SAF leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan 10 April visited Eritrea, met with President Isaias and FM Osman Saleh; leaders likely discussed next phase of Sudan war after SAF regained control of capital Khartoum in March (see Sudan). Meanwhile, presidential adviser Yemane Gebreab 2-3 April travelled to South Sudan, which witnessed recent surge in conflict (see South Sudan), reportedly to deliver message to President Kiir from Isaias; some analysts suspect Gebreab may have warned Juba to refrain from deepening ties with RSF and its backer United Arab Emirates.

Political tensions in Tigray region remained elevated despite a change in the interim administration leadership, while the military stepped up operations against Fano militias in Amhara region and violence persisted in Oromia region. Situation in Tigray remained precarious despite new interim leadership. Abiy 8 April appointed Tigray military commander and VP of outgoing administration, Lt. Gen. Tadesse Werede, as Tigray’s interim president following spike in tensions between interim authorities then headed by Getachew Reda and Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) led by Debretsion Gebremichael. By selecting Tadesse, Abiy bypassed TPLF leaders, likely aiming to consolidate federal influence over key transition issues, notably territorial disputes. In effort to appease TPLF, Tadesse mid-April reinstated three senior army members suspended by Getachew and 21 April named TPLF deputy chairman Amanuel Assefa as his deputy. Easing of political stalemate raised hopes for de-escalation of tensions between Addis Ababa and Asmara amid latter’s meddling in Tigray’s political dispute (see Eritrea). However, tensions in Tigray 26 April rose again when TPLF warned of serious threat to 2022 Pretoria Agreement (which ended war in region) if electoral authorities, due to meet in early May, revoke party’s legal status. News also emerged 27 April that Getachew plans to form new political party, potentially posing serious challenge to TPLF. Military pressure weakened Fano militia in Amhara. Govt stepped up military operations against Fano militia following latter’s offensive in March. Notably, federal forces 21 April claimed hundreds of Fano fighters were killed and several commanders captured during operations across North Shewa and Gojjam zones; local media reported over 100 people killed 17 April in drone strike in East Gojjam’s Gedeb town were civilians, which authorities denied. Oromia continued to face security challenges. Despite decline in large-scale fighting in Oromia, some clashes persisted between Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) and federal forces, sparking retaliatory attacks on civilians. Notably, federal forces 4 April reportedly killed senior OLA commander in Horo Limmu district of East Wollega Zone. In apparent retaliation, OLA 7-12 April allegedly killed dozens of civilians in area, accusing them of colluding with military. Unidentified gunmen in Arzi Zone 29 April reportedly abducted 50 people travelling from Sire district to regional capital Adama.

The security situation remained precarious in the country’s north. Suspected al-Qaeda-affiliated Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM) fighters 9 May attacked police post in Guilmaro town (Atakora department), seizing weapons and freeing prisoners with no reported casualties. Meanwhile, Niger’s President Gen. Tiani 31 May said border with Benin will remain closed for foreseeable future, citing presence of “destabilising French troops” on Beninese territory.

Jihadist militants launched a series of large-scale assaults on army positions and shifted their strategy by seizing secondary towns, leaving hundreds dead and exposing critical weaknesses in the military’s defences. Jihadist militants took control of secondary towns as large-scale attacks on military positions continued. Al-Qaeda-affiliated Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM) 11, 13 May carried out large-scale attacks on Djibo (Sahel region) and Diapaga (East region) towns, respectively, targeting both military and civilian infrastructure; raids reportedly killed at least 200 soldiers and civilian auxiliaries (VDPs) and hundreds of civilians and resulted in temporary takeover of towns by insurgents. Authorities deployed soldiers in Djibo as JNIM withdrew after a few hours, but lacking sufficient air support and equipment, troops appear vulnerable to new JNIM attacks. Diapaga remained under JNIM control through late May. Also, JNIM 6 May launched raid on Lanfiera military camp (Boucle du Mouhoun region), reportedly killing dozens, and 11 May attacked and took control of Sollé military camp (North region), killing at least 60 soldiers. Meanwhile, VDPs in Centre East mid-May issued ultimatum to President Capt. Traoré, threatening to demobilise unless they get reinforced by the military soon. Transitional govt tried to maintain control amid mounting challenges. Faced with pockets of dissent against backdrop of country’s worsening security, military authorities stepped up pro-Traoré propaganda on social media. Meanwhile, several soldiers who have disappeared since April following alleged coup plot remained missing. French daily Le Monde 6 May reported Traoré asked Chad to send 200 soldiers to reinforce his protection force after alleged coup plot. Govt tried to break out of international isolation. Traoré 9 May held talks with Russia’s President Vladimir Putin in Russian capital Moscow; leaders vowed to deepen cooperation. Director general of Iranian police 11 May visited Ouagadougou to discuss police cooperation. Meanwhile, Ambassador to Iran Mohammad Kabura 12 May met with Afghan counterpart Maulvi Fazl Mohammad Haqqani in Iranian capital Tehran, fuelling rumours that Burkina Faso may be seeking closer ties with Taliban authorities with a view to establishing dialogue with JNIM.

The army reported killing 100 members of a Hutu armed group along the border with Rwanda, while the opposition faced mounting repression ahead of the 5 June legislative and communal elections. Military conducted major operations against armed group near Rwandan border. SOS Medias Burundi 9 May reported military between early March and early May had conducted two offensives targeting ethnic Hutu-dominated National Liberation Front (FLN) in Kibira forest, Cibitoke province near Rwandan border; army claimed to have killed over 100 FLN fighters while losing ten soldiers. Authorities said operations against FLN, which refused to integrate into Burundian contingents deployed in eastern DR Congo (DRC), were part of broader effort to stabilise border . Electoral campaign opened in constrained civic space . Arbitrary arrests, disappearances and assaults targeting opposition and media increased. Notably, suspected members of ruling party youth wing Imbonerakure 2 May seriously injured Front for Democracy in Burundi (FRODEBU) activist Jonas Niyomwungere in machete attack in Nyanza-Lac city (Makamba province). Suspected police and Imbonerakure 6 May arrested National Congress for Freedom (CNL) activist Jean-Marie Nizigiyimana in Buterere area on outskirts of Bujumbura city, held him in undisclosed location. NGO Reporters Sans Frontières 8 May accused security forces and Imbonerakure of creating “climate of fear” aimed at silencing independent media ahead of 5 June legislative and communal polls. Meanwhile, authorities 9 May staged ceremony in Gitega city to launch electoral campaign, featuring ruling-party and select opposition speeches. President Ndayishimiye hailed event as democratic milestone. But key opposition figure Agathon Rwasa and Burundi Bwa Bose coalition boycotted, denouncing ruling party’s dominance and citing logistical constraints, notably fuel shortages. After campaign 13 May officially started, Burundi Bwa Bose 15 May and other opposition parties reported obstacles to rallies and other campaign activities, including intimidation and violence. In another important development. SOS Médias Burundi 28 May reported several Congolese refugees had left Musenyi site (Rutana province) to return to DRC amid insufficient access to medical care and food aid.

A legal debate emerged over the eligibility of opposition leader Maurice Kamto in the 5 October presidential election; violence persisted in the Anglophone areas and in the Far North. Political manoeuvring intensified ahead of presidential election scheduled for 5 Oct. Deputy Secretary General of ruling Cameroon People’s Democratic Movement, Grégoire Owona, 14 May said prominent opposition leader Maurice Kamto could be disqualified from presidential race unless nominated as candidate by political party represented in parliament or town councils. Kamto’s party Mouvement pour la Renaissance du Cameroun (MRC), which boycotted 2020 municipal and legislative elections, claims that it fulfils representation criterion through its alliance with MP Jean-Michel Nintcheu and councillors who joined MRC after their election. Political association Groupe de Douala 2 May announced consultations with opposition leaders, including Kamto, aiming to rally behind single candidate. Meanwhile, opposition Parti camerounais pour la réconciliation nationale 23 May chose Cabral Libii as presidential candidate, though dispute with party’s founder Robert Kona continues. Thousands 10 May gathered in Maroua city (Far North region) under banner “100,000 youth united behind [President] Paul Biya in 2025”. Anglophone conflict continued to claim lives in North West (NW) and South West (SW) regions. Anglophone separatists 4 May attacked military outpost in Jakiri town (NW), killing at least one soldier. Roadside bomb attack on armoured patrol vehicle 5 May killed two soldiers in Muyuka commune (SW). Govt forces from 14 May onward arrested dozens of people in Anglophone towns. Several separatist armed groups 19-20 May imposed lockdown across NW and SW regions, aiming to disrupt National Day celebrations, which commemorate 1972 abolition of federation that had granted autonomy to English-speaking West Cameroon; rebels fired warning shots notably in Kumbo town (NW). Insecurity persisted in northern regions. In Far North region, Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) 6 May raided gendarmerie post, army camp and mayor’s residence in Hile Alifa town, Logone-et-Chari division, killing three soldiers and two civilians. In neighbouring Nigeria, ISWAP 16 May attacked Wulgo military base (Borno state), causing casualties among Cameroonian and Nigerian forces. Meanwhile in North region, gunmen 7 May kidnapped Catholic priest in Mayo-Rey division, reportedly demanding ransom, before releasing him 16 May.

Fierce fighting broke out between an ethnic Azandé militia and government and allied forces in the south east; a rebel group excluded from the April truce with the government stepped up hostilities, while violence persisted between the signatories. Violence erupted between ethnic Azandé militia and govt forces in south east. Clashes late April-early May broke out between army and allied Russian paramilitaries on one hand, and Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé Azandé (AAKG) militia on the other, in Zemio town (Haut-Mbomou prefecture), leaving at least 50 dead and dozens injured on both sides. Fighting 6 May spread to Mboki town, killing at least three militiamen. Incidents occurred amid growing tension over militia’s targeting of Fulani civilians and authorities’ decision to disarm 200 Azandé fighters who were integrated into army in 2024. Following clashes, militia 13 May announced agreement with govt, calling on militiamen integrated into army to lay down their arms; however, absence of reintegration plan raises risk that Azandé fighters may continue targeting Fulani communities or turn to banditry. Unidentified gunmen likely to be Azandé militiamen 15 May abducted and killed sub-prefect of Djema (Haut-Mbomou) after he called for deployment of Russian paramilitaries to secure area. Security situation remained precarious despite April truce. In its deadliest attack since at least 2022, ethnic Goula-dominated armed group Party for the Rally of the Central African Nation 14 May raided army position in Ouadda town (Haute-Kotto prefecture in north east), leaving five soldiers, two rebels and two civilians dead; attack may reflect group’s growing sense of marginalisation after govt last month signed ceasefire agreement with two predominantly Fulani armed groups – Union for Peace in the Central African Republic (UPC) and Return, Reclamation and Rehabilitation (3R) – in effort to improve security situation ahead of Dec presidential vote. Tensions also remained high between signatories. 3R fighters 2 May targeted army position in Koundé town (Nana-Mambéré prefecture in west), leaving one civilian and one rebel dead; Russian paramilitaries 7 May killed three UPC fighters near Bria town (Haute-Kotto prefecture in east). At Bangui’s request, Cameroon 5 May extradited Armel Sayo, leader of rebel alliance Military Coalition for People’s Salvation and Recovery.

Deadly clashes between herders and farmers erupted in the country’s south, authorities arrested former Prime Minister Succès Masra and N’Djamena deepened its partnership with Abu Dhabi. Localised violence erupted between farming and herding communities. Farmers and Fulani herders 15 May clashed in Mandakao village (Logone Occidental province); govt reported 42 deaths and six injuries, while local sources claimed 78 people killed and 247 injured. Violence started after local authorities 9 May banned farmers from clearing land, which latter saw as pro-herder, state-backed expropriation, triggering reprisals against herders. Following clashes, security forces allegedly arrested 82 people, mostly farmers; four of them reportedly died in detention. Authorities arrested prominent opposition leader, alleging involvement in violence. Authorities 16 May arrested Succès Masra, former PM and leader of opposition party Les Transformateurs, for allegedly sharing audio message urging farmers in Mandakao to form self-defence groups against herders. Masra denied allegations, saying message was sent two years ago, and his party denounced his arrest as attempt to silence movement. Judge 21 May charged Masra with inciting hatred and revolt, arming militias and complicity in murder and ordered his remand in custody. While Masra has lost credibility and influence among supporters since making series of compromises with President Mahamat Déby in 2023 to become prime minister, he remains troublesome opponent; notably, Masra’s April claim of having signed power-sharing agreement with Déby drew ruling party’s ire. UAE tightened hold on Chad in reaction to Saudi Arabia’s manoeuvres. Chadian authorities 2 May signed agreement with United Arab Emirates (UAE) to deepen trade relations, notably through construction of Chad-Cameroon railway by Emirati company Etihad Rail; also signed deal to build hospital and mosque in capital N’Djamena. Ties intensify amid growing competition between UAE and Saudi Arabia for influence in Chad, against backdrop of tensions over Sudan war. After signs of Chad’s disengagement, Abu Dhabi reportedly threatened to increase interest rate on country’s debt, prompting Déby to visit UAE in April for meeting with President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.

Opposition supporters staged demonstrations to protest the exclusion of Tidjane Thiam from the upcoming October presidential election and demand electoral reforms, while President Ouattara called for “peace and stability”. Pre-electoral tensions persisted as opposition staged protests. Main opposition Democratic Party of Côte d’Ivoire (PDCI) 3-4 May mobilised a few thousand supporters in Abidjan city after court in April ordered removal of Tidjane Thiam, party candidate for 25 Oct presidential election, from electoral register on grounds he had lost Ivorian nationality. Opposition Coalition for Peaceful Change in Côte d’Ivoire – which includes PDCI, Pascal Affi N’Guessan’s Ivorian Popular Front, Simone Ehivet Gbagbo’s Movement of Capable Generations and Charles Blé Goudé’s Pan-African Congress for Justice and Equality of Peoples – 31 May held gathering in Abidjan to protest exclusion of key opposition figures from presidential race and call for electoral roll revision and electoral commission reform. Meanwhile, former minister Jean-Louis Billon 26 May reaffirmed willingness to run as PDCI’s candidate, despite party having named Thiam as its official nominee in April. Amid mounting concern over risk of electoral violence and uncertainty over his potential re-election bid, President Ouattara 22 May said “measures are being taken to ensure peace and stability” and urged Ivorians to “put the national interest first”. Govt discussed strengthening security cooperation with partners. Abidjan moved to bolster its military capabilities amid growing threats from jihadist groups operating in Sahel and increasingly tense relations with Burkina Faso, whose newly acquired air power is reportedly causing concern among Ivorian authorities. Notably, French weekly Jeune Afrique 15 May reported govt in late April held talks with head of U.S. Africa Command, Gen. Michael Langley, on expanding military cooperation. Also, govt 9 May signed military cooperation agreement with Morocco – Côte d’Ivoire’s second-largest military training partner after France.

Amid U.S.-led mediation, Kinshasa and Kigali remained committed to reaching an agreement in June to halt the fighting between Rwanda-backed M23 rebels and Congolese forces in the eastern DR Congo, where M23 stayed on the offensive. M23 failed to make significant advances amid diplomatic pressure. Efforts to reach peace agreement between Kinshasa and Kigali continued under U.S. auspices (see Rwanda). Meanwhile, talks between Rwanda-backed M23 and Congolese govt 4 May resumed in Qatar but progress remained elusive on truce implementation and formal ceasefire. M23 stayed on the offensive in eastern provinces. Notably, rebels around 2 May captured Lunyasenge town on Lake Edward’s west coast in Lubero territory, North Kivu province, and 6 May took Luchiga village in mineral-rich Mwenga territory, South Kivu province. Fighting 14 May broke out between M23 and pro-govt Wazalendo militias in Kalehe territory (South Kivu) and continued through late May as M23 sought to secure Route Nationale 2 linking South Kivu’s capital Bukavu to North Kivu’s capital Goma. M23 mid-May also stepped up offensive in Bwito chiefdom, Rutshuru territory (North Kivu). Other armed groups intensified attacks in eastern province of Ituri. Islamic-state affiliated Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) 6 May killed at least ten people in Irumu territory; assault drew civil society criticism of military’s failure to contain ADF. New militia led by Thomas Lubanga, Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP), early May clashed with army in Djugu territory’s Bahema-Nord chiefdom; army 7 May claimed to have repelled CRP attack on strategic town of Nyamamba near Lake Albert. Also in Djugu, suspected ethnic Lendu CODECO militia 12 May abducted at least 15 civilians in Kirongozi groupement, and 18 May ambushed Ugandan army in Lidda village (see Uganda). Polarisation deepened over eastern conflict. Senate 22 May lifted former President Kabila’s lifetime immunity, clearing way for potential military prosecution over alleged complicity with M23. Security forces same day arrested Kabila’s former mines minister, Martin Kabwelulu, and his former presidential security chief, Gen. Pierre Banywesize, in capital Kinshasa. Kabila 26 May arrived in M23 stronghold of Goma after two years in exile, and 29-30 May consulted with religious and traditional leaders, potentially upsetting delicate negotiations between Kinshasa and M23.

The country won a maritime boundary case against its neighbour Gabon. International Court of Justice (ICJ) 19 May ruled in favour of Equatorial Guinea’s claim over three small islands in potentially oil-rich waters in Gulf of Guinea, ending longstanding territorial dispute with Gabon; ruling means Libreville will have to remove its soldiers from Mbanié island. Gabonese analysts said ICJ accepted Libreville’s demand that some Equatoguinean territories around Mongomo and Ebebiyin towns be returned to Gabon.

The rift in relations with Ethiopia deepened, while Sudan’s paramilitary force launched drone attacks near the border with Eritrea, prompting Asmara to deploy a naval ship to Port Sudan. Tensions with Ethiopia remained high. President Isaias Afwerki’s 24 May Independence Day address laid bare dangerous tensions with Addis Ababa as he accused Ethiopia’s ruling Prosperity Party of promoting an exclusionary ideology that, in his view, endangers national unity and regional stability. He further alleged that foreign powers are exploiting Ethiopia’s post-war fragility through federal govt, which he cast as proxy for external agendas, and warned that Eritrea would not remain passive in face of such provocations . Eritrea deployed naval ship to Port Sudan following drone attacks. Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) early May launched drone strikes in country’s east, notably targeting Port Sudan city north of Eritrea and Kassala city, which lies on country’s western border (see Sudan). In response, Asmara deployed naval ship to Port Sudan to assess situation and also likely due to attacks on Kassala, which Asmara may view as crossing “red lines” communicated to RSF leadership in 2024. While Asmara has mostly restricted its role in Sudan’s war to providing training and some logistical support to army-aligned militias, further RSF attacks in east could trigger increased Eritrean involvement.

The security situation continued to deteriorate as Al-Qaeda-affiliated militants launched their southernmost attack to date; the government denied Niger’s accusation that it is hosting jihadist training camps. Jihadists pushed deeper into Beninese territory. In what appears to be its southernmost attack in country to date, Al-Qaeda-affiliated Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM) 12 June targeted military position in Basso town, Borgou department on border with Nigeria’s Kainji National Park, killing one soldier; JNIM claimed to have taken temporary control of position. Group also continued to target govt forces in northern departments. Notably, security forces 3 June repelled JNIM attack near Birni Lafia town, Alibori department, allegedly killing ten jihadists. Large group of JNIM combatants 4 June raided Tanougou police station, Atacora department, killing at least five security force operatives. After President Talon ordered review of security policy following major jihadist attacks in Jan and April, army chief of staff early June appointed Col. André Dokoui Fofo as new commander of Operation Mirador combating jihadist groups in country’s north since 2022. Tensions with Niger continued to run high. FM Olushegun Adjadi Bakari early June dismissed “unacceptable” allegations after Nigerien President Gen. Tiani 31 May again accused Benin – along with other countries, including Nigeria – of harbouring French military bases to train jihadists with a view to destabilising Niger.

Al-Qaeda-affiliated jihadists scaled back their attacks following a spike in violence since the beginning of 2025; army auxiliaries briefly detained five Ivorian security personnel. Country registered relative lull in jihadist violence. Al-Qaeda-affiliated Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM) conducted smaller-scale assaults compared to previous months. Violence remained widespread, however, with attacks in June killing dozens of soldiers, civilian auxiliary force (VDPs) and civilians in North, Sahel and East regions. Notably, JNIM 1 June attacked Koumbri military camp, Yatenga province (North), and 14-16 June claimed to have taken control of three military posts in Gourma province (East), notably in Nagré and Koaré. Small-scale assaults, including seizure of weapons and capture of VDP posts, were also reported in other regions, notably South-West and Cascades. Meanwhile, army 9 June regained control of military camp in Diapaga city (East region) after JNIM, which had captured site in mid-May, abandoned it. Decline in large-scale attacks does not appear to stem from successful military operations or suggest any structural improvement in overall security situation. Instead, JNIM may have decided to pause effort after unprecedented pace of attacks since beginning of year, or shifted its war effort toward Mali (see Mali). During visit to troops in Centre-South region, President Capt. Traoré 15 June said military operations would intensify and reiterated opposition to any form of dialogue with insurgents. Govt continued nationalising mining sector. In line with country’s revised mining code adopted in July 2024, govt 11 June transferred control of five mines to state-owned company SOPAMIB. In another important development. VDPs 21 June reportedly detained five Ivorian gendarmes at gold mining site in Ivorian border town of Kalamon and transferred them to Burkinabè capital Ouagadougou; Ivorian govt 29 June said officers had been released and returned to Côte d’Ivoire. For more information on possible trends and scenarios from June to November, see our sixth edition of On The Horizon , featuring Burkina Faso.

The ruling party secured a sweeping victory in the communal and legislative elections, consolidating de facto one-party rule amid alleged electoral irregularities; Burundian forces remained active in eastern DR Congo. Ruling party claimed sweeping election win despite reports of irregularities . El ectoral commission 11 June announced ruling CNDD-FDD party had won all 108 National Assembly seats contested in 5 June legislative elections; opposition secured only marginal representation at communal level in local elections held same day. AU observer mission 7 June praised electoral process as peaceful and transparent. However, civil society observers, including Catholic Bishops’ Conference of Burundi, and opposition parties reported widespread irregularities, including voter intimidation, illegal presence of ruling party militia Imbonerakure in polling stations and pre-marked ballots, while SOS-Médias Burundi 10 June denounced systematic media censorship during electoral period. President Ndayishimiye 14 June defended election outcome and warned Church against interference. Intelligence agency next day reportedly arrested Abbé Paul Butoyi, parish priest of Mutumba in Gitaza locality, after sermon perceived as critical of electoral process. Burundian forces remained engaged in eastern DR Congo (DRC). Reports late May-early June emerged of additional Burundian troop deployments to Uvira and Fizi territories in South Kivu province, in support of Congolese forces against M23 rebels and Twirwaneho armed groups. Notably in Fizi highlands, Burundian forces 22 May reportedly advanced toward strategic Bijombo area, and around 9 June allegedly took part in clashes a longside Congolese army and pro-Congolese govt Wazalendo militias in Rugezi area . Reports of Burundian civilians – including refugees living in DRC – joining Wazalendo continued to emerge.

Ahead of the 5 October presidential election, authorities blocked an opposition rally, while President Biya’s support base showed signs of fracturing; meanwhile, Anglophone separatists scaled back their attacks, and violence persisted in the Far North. Political climate continued to heat up ahead of presidential election. Govt forces 7-8 June blocked traffic in parts of economic capital Douala and prevented main opposition party leader and would-be presidential candidate Maurice Kamto from meeting with party members. However, hundreds of Kamto supporters broke through security cordon and gathered in front of party’s local office. Meanwhile, cracks widened within ruling coalition ahead of President Biya’s re-election bid announcement, expected by 12 July. Notably, Biya’s support base in country’s north, which is critical for securing electoral victory, appeared to be fracturing. Employment Minister Issa Tchiroma Bakary – leader of the Cameroon National Salvation Front party – 14 June called on supporters in Garoua city (North region) not to back incumbent, 23 June resigned from govt and 25 June announced presidential candidacy. Tourism Minister Bello Bouba Maïgari, whose National Union for Democracy and Progress party has strong roots in country’s north, 28 June also announced presidential bid. Meanwhile, eight elites from Biya’s native South region 18 June urged fellow southerners to set aside ethnic-based loyalty to Biya in favour of national interest. Anglophone separatists scaled back attacks. After prolonged period of initiating vast majority of attacks, Anglophone separatists launched fewer assaults in June; pullback may be strategic and augur renewed surge of violence closer to presidential election. However, significant incident occurred in francophone West region, which neighbours Anglophone North West and South West regions, as separatist militia 18 June ambushed military patrol truck and killed three soldiers in Magba area. In North West, suspected separatists overnight 29-30 June reportedly killed four soldiers in Wum town. Jihadist attacks on military and civilians continued in Far North . Suspected Islamic State West Africa Province faction of Boko Haram 8 June launched drone strike on Sagmé military post, Logone-et-Chari division near Nigeria border, killing five soldiers. Boko Haram Bakura faction 13 June kidnapped six civilians in Darak town, Logone-et-Chari.

Uncertainty continued to cloud the long-delayed local elections, a suspected Sudanese armed group killed a UN peacekeeper, underscoring the growing spillover of the Sudan conflict, and clashes between armed groups and government forces cast doubt on their commitment to the April truce. Electoral process faced persistent uncertainty. Coalition of civil society groups 4 June raised concern about govt’s failure to publish electoral roll and summon electorate on time for local elections, initially planned for August. Amid severe funding shortfalls, govt appeared intent on organising local vote alongside presidential and legislative elections, currently scheduled for December, to benefit from international actors’ logistical, material and financial support granted only for local elections. Political frictions also continued as govt failed to follow through on April announcement of political dialogue with opposition. UN voiced concern over spillover of Sudan war into north-eastern CAR. In new report to Security Council, UN Sec Gen António Guterres 13 June reported presence of Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in Am Dafok and Aouk areas (Vakaga prefecture). Armed individuals 20 June attacked UN peacekeeping patrol in Am-Sissia 1 village near country’s border with Sudan, killing Zambian peacekeeper; UN 26 June blamed attack on “armed Sudanese elements”, warned that Sudan conflict is spilling across border into Central African Republic. Armed groups and govt forces continued to fight in centre despite April truce. Clashes between suspected Return, Reclamation and Rehabilitation (3R) fighters and national army near Bozoum town (Ouham prefecture) 2 June caused death of four rebels; 3R 4 June accused anti-balaka self-defence militia of killing eight of its fighters in same area. Incidents risk undermining fragile momentum for disarmament generated by April truce between govt and 3R and Union for Peace in the Central African Republic (UPC) armed groups. In modest achievement, Russian paramilitary instructors 13 June disarmed 37 3R combatants in Bossangoa town (Ouham). Violence between Azandé militia and govt and allied forces persisted in south east. Ethnic Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé Azandé (AAKG) militia fighters 1 June ambushed Russian paramilitary patrol near Zémio town (Haut-Mbomou prefecture), killing two. In retaliation, Russian paramilitaries 5 June launched sweep operation in nearby Koumboli village.

The prolonged detention of the opposition leader, former Prime Minister Succès Masra, fuelled political tensions, while deadly violence in the country’s east highlighted the escalating spillover of the Sudan conflict. Calls for opposition leader’s release grew louder, including from within Zaghawa elite. Court 19 June rejected request for provisional release of Succès Masra, former PM and leader of opposition party Les Transformateurs, who was arrested in May for alleged involvement in deadly herder-farmer clashes in Mandakao village (Logone-Occidental province). Masra 24 June launched hunger strike to protest detention, before ending it 30 June, citing medical reasons. Masra’s supporters throughout June held regular press conferences at party’s headquarters in capital N’Djamena and maintained active online presence to denounce what they described as politically motivated effort to silence their leader; about 30 women 28 June also demanded “freedom for Masra” outside party headquarters. Former presidential adviser and prominent ethnic Zaghawa figure Abderahmane Haggar late June called for Masra’s release. Herder-farmer violence continued in south. Suspected Fulani herders 19 June attacked Oregomel village (Mayo-Kebbi Ouest province), killing at least 19 people, mostly women; authorities arrested 20 assailants. Incident took place 5km from Mandakao, where herder-farmer clashes left at least 42 people dead in May. War in Sudan fuelled deadly violence in east. Gunmen 10 June killed ten people in Molou canton (Ouaddaï province) in what local sources described as revenge attack by former fighters recently returned from Sudan. Suspected members of pro-govt militia known as Defence, Intelligence and Support 14 June opened fire on civilians in same area, killing up to 40 people. Attacks, which are unprecedented in scale and nature, raised concerns about security forces’ capacity to contain spillover effects of Sudan’s conflict, which has led to influx of former combatants and proliferation of weapons in eastern Chad. Criminal violence intensified along trade routes. Notably, gunmen 1 June ambushed trade convoy in Niellim canton (Moyen-Chari province), killing five civilians. Local sources attributed assault to former rebels of Movement for Peace, Reconstruction and Development, who have engaged in criminal activities since group disbanded.

The final electoral list confirmed the exclusion of opposition leader Tidjane Thiam from the presidential polls scheduled for October, sparking peaceful protests; Burkinabè army auxiliaries briefly detained Ivorian soldiers. Thousands protested exclusion of opposition leader from presidential race. Electoral commission 4 June published final electoral roll, confirming absence from presidential race of four opposition figures, including Tidjane Thiam, president of main opposition Democratic Party of Côte d’Ivoire (PDCI), former President Laurent Gbagbo, head of African People’s Party-Côte d’Ivoire (PPA-CI), Gbagbo’s former right-hand man Charles Blé Goudé, and former PM Guillaume Soro. In response, several thousand PDCI activists 14 June demonstrated in Abidjan city to protest decision. Gbagbo and Thiam 19 June also announced formation of “common front” between PPA-CI and PDCI, calling for reinstatement of candidates, audit of electoral roll and reform of electoral body. President Ouattara maintained uncertainty over candidacy for upcoming vote. Ruling Rally of Houphouëtists for Democracy and Peace (RHDP) 21 June nominated Ouattara as party’s candidate for presidential election. Ouattara next day addressed supporters in Abidjan city but did not confirm his candidacy, stating he would make decision in “coming days”. Burkinabè forces detained Ivorian gendarmes. Burkinabè civilian auxiliary force (VDPs) 21 June reportedly detained five Ivorian gendarmes at gold mining site in Ivorian border town of Kalamon and transferred them to Burkinabè capital Ouagadougou; Ivorian govt 29 June said officers had been released and returned to Côte d’Ivoire.

Kinshasa and Kigali signed a long-awaited peace agreement, offering a chance to end three years of conflict between Rwandan-backed M23 rebels and Congolese forces in the eastern DR Congo (DRC), though significant challenges to its implementation persist. Agreement with Kigali raised hopes for peace. Congolese and Rwandan FMs 27 June signed U.S. and Qatar-brokered peace agreement in U.S. capital, Washington, DC; deal calls on belligerents to cease hostilities, respect their neighbour’s territorial integrity, halt support to non-state armed groups and set up joint monitoring and security mechanisms; under its terms, Rwandan soldiers are to withdraw from eastern DRC within three months. Presidential summit in the U.S. expected in coming months to seal agreement. Concerns over peace prospects persisted, however, as Rwandan-backed M23 rebels, who retain control of strategic areas in DRC, described deal as bilateral pact which did not involve them. Meanwhile, Qatar-mediated talks between M23 and Kinshasa continued with minimal progress. M23 continued to battle fragmented foes in Kivu provinces . Heavy fighting 15-17 June erupted in Rutshuru territory, North Kivu, between M23 and pro-govt forces including Wazalendo militias, notably in Bambo, Bukombo and Tongo towns; violence left dozens dead and thousands displaced. Clashes 18 June spread to outskirts of neighbouring province South Kivu’s capital Bukavu, notably Panzi, Nyantende-Kasihe and Bagira towns. Also in South Kivu, govt forces and Wazalendo allies around 9 June clashed with M23-Twirwaneho-Red Tabara coalition in Rugezi area of Fizi highlands, fuelling displacement toward Uvira town. Army 30 June struck and destroyed small plane heading toward Minembwe town in South Kivu for allegedly violating Congolese airspace; M23 denounced “crime” against humanitarian aircraft. Political polarisation continued to grow . Transport Minister Jean-Pierre Bemba 9 June accused former President Kabila of treason and efforts to destabilise state using M23 conflict. Move appeared aimed at reaffirming loyalty to President Tshisekedi, while sidelining opposition figure Moïse Katumbi and Church leaders, who have pushed for national dialogue. Meanwhile, former ruling party leader Jean-Marc Kabund 19 June launched new opposition platform, Coalition of the Congolese Left, vowing to break with “old order” and urging dialogue with Rwanda and among Congolese to address crisis in east and restore national cohesion.

Tensions with Addis Ababa soared as Asmara intensified its engagement with Ethiopia’s Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Tensions with Addis Ababa escalated. Ethiopian FM Gedion Timotheos 20 June circulated letter to diplomatic community, seen by Crisis Group, accusing Eritrea of undermining Ethiopia’s sovereignty and obstructing conflict resolution efforts in its Tigray region. Letter alleged that Eritrean forces are still occupying Ethiopian territory, committing violence against civilians, and collaborating with TPLF factions and other groups to undertake “major offensive operation during the upcoming rainy season”, which lasts from around June-Sept. Eritrea 26 June issued rebuttal, accusing Addis Ababa of launching “diplomatic campaign to falsely accuse Eritrea of provocations while preparing for conflict”. Mutual recriminations mark serious escalation in tensions, fuelling fears of possible military confrontation. Rapprochement between Asmara and TPLF continued. Debretsion Gebremichael, leader of TPLF (dominant party in Ethiopia’s Tigray region), 1 June publicly congratulated Eritrea on its independence anniversary. Residents of Gulemekheda (Zalambesa area of Tigray) same day reportedly crossed into Eritrea to join Independence Day celebrations in Ambesetegheleba (Senafe area of Southern Zone of Eritrea). Eritrean and TPLF-affiliated social media personalities 22 June also orchestrated meet-up of civilians at bridge over Mereb river, which marks border, near Ethiopia’s Zalambesa town. Growing engagement between historic foes came as both TPLF’s and Asmara’s relations with Ethiopia’s federal govt worsen. In another important development. After deploying naval ship to Port Sudan in May,Asmara refrained from further action in response to drone attacks by Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces near Eritrean border.

The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) moved toward a rapprochement with Eritrea as tensions between Addis Ababa and Asmara soared; the insurgencies in Oromia and Amhara regions persisted. Asmara strengthened ties with TPLF as tensions with Addis Ababa soared. TPLF leader Debretsion Gebremichael 1 June publicly congratulated Eritrea on its independence anniversary, while Asmara during month orchestrated cross-border gatherings of Tigray and Eritrea residents (see Eritrea). Rapprochement between historic foes comes amid their worsening ties with Ethiopia’s federal govt. Notably, FM Gedion Timotheos 20 June circulated letter to diplomatic community, seen by Crisis Group, accusing Eritrea of undermining Ethiopia’s sovereignty and obstructing conflict resolution efforts. Letter alleged that Eritrean forces are still occupying Ethiopian territory, committing violence against civilians, and collaborating with TPLF factions and other groups to undertake “major offensive operation during the upcoming rainy season”, which lasts from around June-Sept. Eritrea 26 June issued rebuttal, accusing Addis Ababa of launching “diplomatic campaign to falsely accuse Eritrea of provocations while preparing for conflict”. Mutual recriminations mark serious escalation in tensions, raising fears of possible military confrontation. Insurgencies in Amhara and Oromia regions continued. In Amhara, newly-created umbrella organisation Amhara Fano National Force (AFNF) 26 June announced formation of new committees aimed at coordinating Fano insurgency and strengthening internal cohesion. Fano leaders in Gojjam area, however, distanced themselves from committee, indicating AFNF already faces internal divisions. Still fighting continued, with notable uptick in combat reported late June in Gojjam. In Oromia, approximately 20 Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) fighters reportedly operating in Guji and Borena zones 11 June surrendered to govt forces, possibly signalling attrition within OLA ranks in some areas. Even so, clashes with federal forces continued across region, including in Kellem Wollega, West Arsi and South West Shewa zones. In another important development. Intelligence chief Gen. Redwan Hussein 1 June delivered official letter from PM Abiy to Sudanese army leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan during visit to Port Sudan city; Addis Ababa likely voiced concern over ongoing rapprochement between Sudanese army and Eritrea, and latter’s possible direct involvement in Sudan’s conflict (see Eritrea, Sudan).

Protests over fuel price hikes left at least 22 people dead in the capital, Luanda. Thousands 28-29 July joined taxi drivers demonstrating in capital Luanda against increase in fuel prices; amid reports of vandalism and looting, clashes erupted between police and protesters, with sporadic gunfire heard in parts of city. Govt 30 July said violence left at least 22 dead, including police officer, and 197 injured; authorities also arrested over 1,120 people. Calm returned to Luanda by 30 July, but unrest reportedly spread notably to central Huambo province. Violence followed weeks of student-led protests over rising tuition fees and cost of living, amid widespread discontent with govt austerity measures.

The country experienced a lull in jihadist violence, and the government reiterated its commitment to military cooperation with Côte d’Ivoire. Army continued to step up pressure on jihadist groups in country’s north. Following series of large-scale jihadist attacks since early 2025, military from late June onward conducted several operations against al-Qaeda-affiliated Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM) in northern departments, in particular Point Triple area near border with Burkina Faso and Niger. Amid military pressure, country in July registered lull in jihadist violence. Benin and Côte d’Ivoire discussed deepening security cooperation. Senior army officers from Benin and Côte d’Ivoire 17 July met in Ivorian city of Abidjan to strengthen military cooperation in face of security threats, particularly from jihadist groups. Meeting further underscores growing prioritisation of bilateral initiatives over regional security frameworks amid escalating tensions in West Africa, notably between Benin and Niger. In another important development. Govt late July invited troops from Alliance of Sahel States (AES) – Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger – to attend upcoming National Day military parade on 1 Aug; gesture could signal Benin’s readiness to mend relations with AES countries.

Al-Qaeda-affiliated jihadists intensified their attacks following a weeks-long lull; meanwhile, the death of a Burkinabè influencer in Côte d’Ivoire heightened tensions between the two countries. Jihadist attacks surged after relative lull in early June. In Centre-North region, al-Qaeda-affiliated Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM) 28 July attacked military base in Dargo town (Namentenga province), reportedly killing about 50 soldiers; raid and other JNIM attacks on military positions south of Kaya city (Sanmatenga province) since late June suggest group’s growing territorial ambition. In East region, JNIM intensified pressure on Fada N’Gourma (Gourma province) in apparent bid to isolate town from capital Ouagadougou by attacking its western approaches; attacks on town itself included daring raid on Fada University 19 July. In response, military early July conducted joint counter-insurgency operations with Niger in Ougarou area of neighbouring Gnagna province. Meanwhile, JNIM carried out major offensive in Boucle du Mouhoun region (west), with series of highly lethal and well-coordinated attacks involving ambushes and assaults on military and civilian auxiliary forces (VDPs) positions. Notably, militants 11 July killed 16 VDPs in ambush near Dédougou town (Mouhoun province), and 17 July killed 13 soldiers and seven VDPs near Dédougou and Lankoué town (Sourou province). Sahel region (north) saw renewed clashes between JNIM and Islamic State Sahel Province, including 7-8 July near Sebba town ( Yagha province) , Gorgadji town and Bambofa village (both Séno province). Authorities dissolved electoral commission, maintained pressure on critics. Govt 16 July passed bill to dissolve Independent National Electoral Commission, citing financial constraints and concerns over potential foreign interference; body’s powers were transferred to public security ministry. Meanwhile, authorities 11-21 July released at least eight people – including at least five journalists and two civil society actors critical of military rule – who had been detained for up to two years. Security forces 26-27 July briefly detained veteran political figure Hermann Yaméogo after he published article criticising current security policy. In other important developments. Govt 29 July accused Ivorian authorities of “assassination” after Burkinabè influencer Alain Traoré was found dead in his prison cell in Côte d’Ivoire (see Côte d’Ivoire). Demonstrations demanding “justice” late July took place in Ouagadougou.

President Ndayishimiye dismissed concerns over the integrity of the legislative and local elections held in June, as the country continued its drift toward de facto one-party rule. Ruling party consolidated power across all levels, branches of govt. Electoral commission 25 July announced ruling CNDD-FDD party had won all 10 Senate seats in indirect elections held 23 July; Constitutional Court 29 July confirmed results. One-party National Assembly inaugurated 28 July following elections held in June; in breach of constitutional provisions, three govt ministers elected as MPs took their seats in chamber. In further sign of Burundi’s drift toward de facto one-party state, Senate 3 July approved appointment of five new provincial governors, all ruling party members, following territorial reorganisation that reduced number of provinces from 18 to five. Opposition’s efforts to draw international attention to electoral irregularities backfired. During celebrations marking anniversary of Burundi’s independence, President Ndayishimiye 1 July accused opposition of acting under influence of former colonial powers; comment came after opposition, including National Congress for Freedom party and Burundi Bwa Bose coalition, urged him in letter also sent to AU, East African Community, and UN to address their concerns about 5 June legislative and municipal elections, including expulsion of observers and lack of transparency in vote-counting process. Threat of M23 offensive near Burundi’s border kept army on high alert. Kinshasa 11 July warned of imminent Rwanda-backed M23/Congo River Alliance (AFC) offensive on Congolese town of Uvira in South Kivu province. Amid fear of attack, several South Kivu officials reportedly started spending nights in Burundi’s economic capital Bujumbura, located few kilometres from Uvira. Spread of conflict into Uvira would significantly heighten risk of spillover into Burundi. In another important development. AU 17 July named Ndayishimiye, who will assume AU leadership in Feb 2026, as Sahel special envoy; appointment confirms success of Ndayishimiye’s efforts to end Burundi’s international isolation.

In the lead-up to the 12 October vote, President Biya announced his bid for re-election, while electoral authorities barred the main opposition candidate, Maurice Kamto, from running; Anglophone separatists pledged to obstruct the vote. Biya launched re-election bid, consolidated control over security forces . Biya 11 July called presidential election for 12 Oct and 13 July announced his candidacy; move ends months-long speculation that Biya, whose involvement in state affairs has declined in recent years, may withdraw from politics due to his advanced age (92) and deepening fractures within ruling coalition. Meanwhile, Biya 15 July issued presidential decrees reshuffling military top ranks across armed forces in apparent attempt to consolidate power ahead of vote. Electoral commission barred Biya’s main challenger from presidential race. Opposition leader Maurice Kamto mid-July submitted candidacy for presidential election after opposition Mouvement Africain pour la Nouvelle Indépendance et la Démocratie (MANIDEM) endorsed him; Kamto could not file candidacy through his own Mouvement pour la Renaissance du Cameroun (MRC) due to party’s lack of elected officials following 2020 election boycott. Electoral commission 26 July, however, rejected Kamto’s candidacy after rival MANIDEM faction presented another candidate; Kamto 28 July filed appeal with Constitutional Council. Amid fears of unrest, security forces late July reportedly deployed in capital Yaoundé, notably around electoral commission headquarters, and in economic capital Douala. Anglophone separatists vowed to block elections. Following Biya’s announcement, pro-Ambazonia separatist leaders declared voting “outlawed in their land” and threatened to implement lockdown in Anglophone regions between 1 and 12 October to prevent voting. Separatists rejected calls from francophone politicians to allow voting as means to oust Biya; instead, separatist leader Chris Anu demanded Anglophone prisoner releases, ceasefire and talks with govt as pre-conditions for elections. Meanwhile, violence continued. Notably, Anglophone rebels 2 July killed two soldiers and seized weapons in Muyuka town (South West) and 4 July killed police officer in Bafanji village (North West). Jihadist attacks persisted in Far North region, with series of civilian kidnappings . Boko Haram insurgents 1-15 July launched around a dozen attacks across Mayo-Sava, Mayo-Tsanaga and Logone-et-Chari divisions, abducting over 30 civilians, including numerous children.

President Touadéra announced his candidacy for a third term, two prominent rebel leaders declared the dissolution of their movements, and the Sudanese conflict continued to destabilise the country’s north east. Ruling party named Touadéra as its presidential candidate . Touadéra 26 July accepted ruling United Hearts Movement’s nomination as presidential candidate, paving way for third term under new constitution adopted in 2023. Meanwhile, in audio recording leaked 7 July, senior official from UN mission MINUSCA expressed doubts about country’s ability to organise presidential and legislative elections in Dec, citing operational hurdles. In response, opposition coalition Republican Bloc for the Defence of the Constitution called on mission to suspend electoral support until electoral body is reformed. Govt 11 July reaffirmed commitment to holding polls this year, said municipal elections scheduled for August would be held alongside other ballots in Dec; arrangement may be intended to circumvent budget shortfalls by tapping into international funds earmarked exclusively for local vote. Two major rebel group leaders laid down their arms . Ali Darassa, founder of Unity for Peace in the Central African Republic (UPC), and Sembé Bobo, commander of Return, Reclamation and Reintegration (3R), 10 July announced dissolution of respective movements. Major symbolic step, which was announced during ceremony held in capital Bangui to formalise April truce between both armed groups and govt, may not translate into halt of hostilities, however, as thousands of fighters across country may refuse to lay down weapons in absence of credible disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration process. Insecurity continued to rise along Sudan’s border . In context of mounting tensions between local Gula, Kara and Sara communities, on one hand, and Arabs arriving from Sudan on the other, unidentified gunmen, described by local sources as Arab bandits, 2 July stole motorcycle belonging to local official near Birao town (Vakaga prefecture), prompting local youths to pursue attackers, leaving unknown number of casualties. Presumed members of Arab militia 8-10 July also reportedly attacked village near Birao, setting fire to at least ten houses. Amid growing insecurity, Vakaga branch of Central African Women’s Organisation 1 July urged authorities to temporarily ban movement of Sudanese herders around Birao and provide military training to local youths.

President Déby reshuffled key security institutions amid rising insecurity in the east and tensions within the ruling elite over the war in Sudan, while competition over resources continued to fuel violence in the south. Authorities reshuffled security personnel amid spillover of Sudan’s war . President Déby 23 July reshuffled key security institutions, including heads of police, gendarmerie and intelligence agency, appointing mostly officials from his Zaghawa ethnic group. Shift appears tied to struggles for institutional control between Zaghawa and Arab elites amid mounting tensions over Déby’s alleged support for Sudan’s predominantly Arab paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Despite mounting violence near Sudanese border in east, where pro-govt militia allegedly killed 50 civilians in June, security minister – Arab general allegedly close to RSF – was kept in post. Reshuffle may reflect balancing act – offering concessions to Zaghawa while keeping strategic control largely in hands of Goranes and Arabs to appease United Arab Emirates, which backs RSF. Resource competition continued to fuel violence in south . Unidentified armed individuals 4 July stole herd of cattle from farmers in Bouna sub-prefecture (Moyen-Chari province); residents and security forces pursued perpetrators and recovered cattle near border with Central African Republic. Violent clash 10 July also broke out between farmers from two neighbouring villages in Bébidja sub-prefecture (Logone Oriental province) over long-standing land dispute, leaving one dead and 13 injured. Meanwhile, PM Allamaye Halina 8 July brokered peace deal in Mandakao village (Logone-Occidental province) after herder-farmer clashes in May left over 40 Fulanis dead; parties committed to transforming Fulani settlement camps into permanent villages, equitably distributing arable land between herders and farmers, and ensuring justice and reparations for Fulani victims. Move reinforced perception of govt’s pro-herder bias, with local media describing agreement as imposed peace, while local farmers criticised it as favouring herders. Detained opposition leader sought to garner international support . Lawyers of opposition leader Succès Masra – arrested in May for alleged involvement in herder-farmer violence – early July sent formal letter to French President Macron, urging him to speak out in support of Masra, and 17 July denounced case as “political conspiracy”.

President Ouattara announced his candidacy for a fourth term in the October presidential election amid mounting tensions with the opposition; meanwhile, the death of a Burkinabè national in detention further strained relations with Ouagadougou. Ouattara declared himself presidential candidate as govt-opposition tensions continued to rise . In televised speech, President Ouattara, 83, 29 July said he will stand for fourth term in 25 Oct poll, stating that managing growing regional security threats and global economic uncertainties “requires experience”. Opposition quickly criticised long-anticipated announcement, with main opposition Democratic Party of Côte d’Ivoire (PDCI) – whose leader Tidjane Thiam was barred from running in presidential election following court ruling – calling it unconstitutional. Earlier, authorities 2, 8 July arrested four young PDCI leaders and charged them with “disturbing public order” for posting video online in May calling on supporters to take to the streets. Meanwhile, officials from ruling Rally of Houphouëtists for Democracy and Peace 16 July met in Abidjan city with opposition Coalition for a Pacific Change in Côte d’Ivoire representatives to discuss electoral matters, but absence of two key founders of alliance, PDCI and Pascal Affi N’Guessan’s Ivorian Popular Front (FPI), highlighted divisions within opposition. Burkinabè influencer died in custody, further straining relations with Ouagadougou . Public prosecutor 26 July announced death in detention of Burkinabè influencer close to Burkina Faso’s military authorities, Alain Traoré, who was arrested in Côte d’Ivoire in Jan on spying allegations. Ouagadougou 29 July denounced “assassination”, rejecting Ivorian authorities’ statement that activist died by suicide. Côte d’Ivoire and Benin discussed strengthening military cooperation . Senior army officers from Côte d’Ivoire and Benin 17 July met in Abidjan to consolidate military cooperation in face of cross-border security threats. Meeting further underscores growing prioritisation of bilateral initiatives over regional security frameworks amid escalating tensions in West Africa.

Violence escalated in Ituri province, leaving over 140 dead; Kinshasa and the Rwanda-backed M23 rebels pledged to sign a comprehensive peace agreement by mid-August, while also reinforcing their positions in South Kivu province, heightening fears of an imminent battle for Uvira city. Various armed group wreaked havoc in Ituri province, leaving over 140 dead . Islamic State-affiliated Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) 8-12 and 27 July killed at least 123 people in Ituri and neighbouring North Kivu provinces, including during attack on Catholic church in Komanda town, Irumu territory. Fighting between ethnic Lendu CODECO and ethnic Hema Zaïre militias 21 July reportedly left at least 21 dead in Lopa and Nizi localities, Djugu territory, despite late-June agreement to cease hostilities. Meanwhile, Thomas Lubanga’s Convention pour la Révolution Populaire and allied Zaïre militia throughout July clashed with army in Djugu and Irumu. M23 and Kinshasa signed declaration of principles to end fighting, marking important step toward peace . Under Qatari auspices, Congolese govt and Rwanda-backed M23/Congo River Alliance (AFC) rebels 19 July signed roadmap to peace, committing to permanent ceasefire, civilian protection and return of displaced populations.
