Declaration of Principles does not address central issue of M23 territorial control in Kivu provinces, however, which could derail formal peace negotiations set to begin by 8 Aug, with aim of reaching long-awaited comprehensive agreement by 18 Aug (see Rwanda). M23 conflict continued in Kivu provinces, reportedly killing 169 civilians . Reports of M23/AFC troop movements in South Kivu, notably toward Uvira territory’s Katogota village via Kamanyola groupement (Walungu territory), early July fuelled fear of imminent offensive on Uvira city near Burundi (see Burundi). In response, armed forces 11 July underwent sweeping restructuring, and military and allies 13 July launched counteroffensive, with clashes concentrated in Kahololo, Katogota, Rugezi, Minembwe and Bijabo areas. Fighting also continued in North Kivu. Notably, heavy clashes reported 28 July between M23 rebels and govt-aligned Wazalendo militias around Ngululu and Ndete villages in Masisi territory. UN Joint Human Rights Office said M23 from 9 July onwards killed 169 farmers and other civilians in Rutshuru territory. Meanwhile, authorities in July reportedly detained several high-ranking army officers, including ex-army chief Gen. Christian Tshiwewe and head of presidential security Gen. Franck Ntumba, highlighting fears of coup.

Tensions over Addis Ababa’s quest for sea access, coupled with turmoil in Ethiopia’s Tigray region, added to fears of renewed conflict between the two neighbours. In televised address, President Isaias 19 July criticised Ethiopia’s renewed focus on securing sea access as “infantile, dangerous adventurism” and intimated that bigger players were behind these manoeuvres, particularly United Arab Emirates. Citing allegations that Ethiopia is stockpiling weapons, Isaias cautioned neighbouring country against return to war, warning that Eritrea would not be easily overpowered despite Ethiopia’s numerical superiority. Isaias’s interview came after Ethiopia’s PM Abiy Ahmed 3 July reiterated in address to parliament that country’s landlocked status undermines its sovereignty. This fraught situation, coupled with rising tensions in Tigray region between Ethiopia’s federal govt and Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) – which has forged closer ties with Asmara – continued to fuel fears of renewed conflict (see Ethiopia).

The ruling coalition chose the finance minister as its candidate for the 2026 presidential election; the lull in jihadist violence continued, with no major attacks reported. Ruling coalition overnight 30-31 Aug picked Economy Minister Romuald Wadagni as its candidate for 2026 presidential election; move confirms President Talon, who has been in power since 2016, will not seek third term.

Jihadists continued their spate of attacks on the security forces; Ouagadougou expelled a UN official but saw warming ties with Washington. Violence remained widespread, while intra-jihadist clashes occurred. Northern areas saw brunt of jihadist attacks in Aug. In North region, al-Qaeda-affiliated Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM) 13 Aug attacked army base in Youba commune, Yatenga province, reportedly killing 20 soldiers. In Sahel region (north), Islamic State Sahel Province (IS-Sahel) 17 Aug reportedly killed some 15 army auxiliaries (VDPs) near Gorom-Gorom town (Oudalan province). Jihadists groups also engaged in clashes in Sahel region. Notably, IS-Sahel 8 Aug attacked JNIM base in Yagha province and 14 Aug reportedly killed JNIM fighter in Seno province. Violence also persisted elsewhere. In East region, JNIM 20 Aug claimed to have overrun Foutouri army base in Komondjari province near Niger border, although govt sources said they repelled attack. Civic space continued to shrink as authorities suspended radio station. Media authorities 2 Aug suspended private radio broadcaster Omega for three months after journalist referred to govt as “junta”. Although three journalists forcibly enrolled in security forces released in July, at least three others thought to be at frontlines remained missing. Incidents along border with Côte d’Ivoire threatened to fuel bilateral tensions. VDPs 24 Aug detained six Ivorian govt officials on mission in Côte d’Ivoire’s Bounkani region near border with Burkina Faso, transferring them to Ouagadougou. Ivorian media also blamed 25 Aug attack that killed four people in Difita village (also Bounkani) on VDPs (see Côte d’Ivoire). Govt expelled UN official, but undertook diplomacy with U.S. Authorities 18 Aug declared UN Resident Coordinator Carol Flore-Smereczniak persona non grata in protest at UN report published in March documenting impact of Burkina Faso’s conflict on children; UN delegation 25-27 Aug visited Ouagadougou in attempt to repair ties. As alliance with Moscow remained strong, signs of thaw in relations with U.S. continued to emerge. After President Capt. Traoré’s close aide, Brig. Gen. Kassoum Coulibaly, in July took office as new ambassador to U.S., FM Karamoko Jean-Marie Traoré 18 Aug met with U.S. ambassador to Ouagadougou, who said U.S. congressional delegation would visit soon.

President Ndayishimiye cemented his grip on power with a new cabinet, while the conflict in neighbouring DR Congo (DRC) continued to threaten the stability of his regime. Ndayishimiye placed loyalists in key positions as part of power consolidation drive. Ndayishimiye 5 Aug announced new, reduced 13-member cabinet with former Finance Minister Nestor Ntahontuye as PM and former police chief Léonidas Ndaruzaniye as interior minister. Upper house of parliament same day elected outgoing PM Gervais Ndirakobuca as Senate president. Previously, Ndayishimiye had reportedly sought to instal Ndaruzaniye as president of lower house of parliament, but MPs late July re-elected incumbent Gélase Daniel Ndabirabe, who enjoys support of ruling party’s old guard, including army generals. Meanwhile, National Intelligence Service 21 Aug arrested Police Brig. Gen. Bertin Gahungu in economic capital Bujumbura allegedly on accusations of “undermining internal security” and “insulting the Head of State”. Local polls – final stage of 2025 elections that have seen Burundi drift toward de facto one-party rule – held 25 Aug amid reports of electoral irregularities including ballot box stuffing. Fighting across border in DRC continued to unsettle govt. Rwandan-backed M23 rebels in Aug continued to mobilise around Congolese border town of Uvira, where thousands of Burundian soldiers are based. Amid reports that Burundian troops deployed in DRC are underpaid, underequipped and demoralised, members of ruling party youth wing Imbonerakure returning from DRC around 12 Aug told SOS Médias Burundi they had also not been paid. Diplomat Edouard Bizimana, known for his hardline stance against Rwanda, 5 Aug became FM as part of govt reshuffle (see above), further reducing prospects for rapprochement with Kigali. Meanwhile, BBC News 4 Aug reported M23 and Burundi late July exchanged prisoners of war. In another important development. Police 20 Aug arrested head of opposition Council of Patriots party, Anicet Niyonkuru, on fraud allegations.

The Constitutional Council upheld the decision to bar opposition leader Maurice Kamto from contesting the 12 October presidential election, while Anglophone separatist and jihadist attacks persisted. In absence of opposition leader, northern politicians vied to be President Biya’s main challenger. Constitutional Council 5 Aug rejected Kamto’s appeal challenging electoral body’s decision to bar him from presidential race. Small protests in support of Kamto reported 4-5 Aug in capital Yaoundé, with police allegedly firing tear gas. With Kamto out of race, northern politicians Bello Bouba Maigari and Issa Tchiroma Bakary – who resigned from govt in June – emerged as Biya’s main challengers. Thousands 15 Aug greeted Tchiroma upon his return to North region’s capital Garoua, while Bouba 22 Aug addressed thousands of supporters during rally in Adamawa regional capital N’Gaoundéré; skirmish next day erupted in Meiganga town between govt official who tried to block Bouba’s convoy and local supporters. Other prominent opposition candidates, including Cabral Libii and Joshua Osih, appeared to lose ground but resisted calls to unite behind single candidate. Doubts persisted over Biya’s capacity to serve another mandate. Opposition candidate Akere Muna 19 Aug submitted petition to Constitutional Council seeking to disqualify Biya from presidential race, citing constitutional provision that bars candidates who are dependent on others; council 22 Aug rejected petition. Separatist attacks continued notably in Anglophone North West region . Suspected Anglophone separatists 11 and 18 Aug ambushed army patrols respectively in Mah village, Boyo division, and Nwa town, Donga-Mantung division, leaving at least four dead. Meanwhile, security forces 19 Aug reportedly killed two civilians, including pregnant woman, at checkpoint in North West regional capital Bamenda. Govt forces late Aug reinforced deployment in both North West and South West regions as separatist rebels 26 Aug announced lockdown in both regions from 8 Sept to 14 Oct to disrupt presidential election. Jihadist violence targeted civilians in Far North region . Series of civilian kidnappings by suspected Boko Haram insurgents continued, including 14 Aug on Kousseri-Maroua road (Logone-et-Chari division) and 26 Aug in Mora locality (Mayo-Sava division). Insurgents 16 Aug also attacked Djibrili village (Mayo-Tsanaga division), killing one civilian and injuring five.

Authorities scheduled general elections for 28 December, members of the rebel groups that had signed a truce with the government continued to pose a security threat, and Abu Dhabi further consolidated its presence in the country. Authorities unveiled electoral schedule. Electoral commission 5 Aug announced that first round of presidential and legislative elections, and single-round regional and municipal polls, will take place on 28 Dec; 23 Aug published final electoral roll, with 2.4mn registered voters. Election body continued to face numerous logistical and financial challenges in run-up to votes, however, while opposition’s participation in elections remained uncertain amid concerns about reliability of electoral list. After govt 6 Aug said it was committed to promoting inclusive electoral process, opposition coalition Republican Bloc for the Defence of the Constitution denounced communication tactic aimed at appeasing donors. Insecurity persisted despite peace deal with rebels. President Touadéra 6 Aug said 375 rebels had disarmed since Return, Reclamation and Reintegration (3R) and Unity for Peace in the Central African Republic (UPC) rebel group leaders in July announced laying down their arms during ceremony formalising April truce with govt.Thousands of fighters continue to pose security threat across country, however, as deal offers little to combatants, most of whom want to join army despite govt’s plan to reintegrate them into civilian life. Several incidents involving 3R elements reported in country’s north west. Notably, 3R members opposed to disarmament process 13, 14 Aug attacked two local officials in Lim-Pendé prefecture, and 21 Aug injured at least three civilians in Ouham-Bac town (Ouham prefecture). 3R 18 Aug also accused Russian paramilitaries of violating agreement by attacking group’s positions in Nana- Mambéré and Ouham-Pendé prefectures. Meanwhile, govt forces 3 Aug launched raid on anti-balaka militia in Aba-Gobani village (Nana-Mambéré); clashes left one soldier dead. United Arab Emirates (UAE) ramped up investments in CAR. Touadéra 13 Aug launched construction of solar field near capital Bangui, financed by $90mn investment from UAE, reflecting Abu Dhabi’s growing foothold in CAR. Facing severe financial difficulties, Touadéra may be open to allowing UAE to use CAR as supply route for Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in exchange for financial support.

The political space shrank further as a court handed former Prime Minister Succès Masra a 20-year prison sentence, while the death of a state official in suspicious circumstances caused trouble amid a growing crackdown on dissent. Opposition leader sentenced to twenty years in jail . Court 9 Aug sentenced former PM and opposition leader Succès Masra to 20 years in prison for complicity in murder, disseminating hate speech and inciting xenophobia. NGO Human Rights Watch 12 Aug said trial was part of broader pattern of shrinking political space in Chad. Verdict is likely to further weaken opposition and could exacerbate divisions within Masra’s party, Les Transformateurs. Notably, Masra 9 Aug temporarily handed over party leadership to former VP of African Development Bank, Bedoumra Kordjé, fuelling tensions over growing influence of Ngambaye community within party leadership structure. Death of state official in unclear circumstances stirred speculation of state crime. Fulbert Mouanodji, former chief of staff to governor of Ennedi-Est province (east), 2 Aug died from severe burns in Ouaddaï provincial capital Abéché (also east). Circumstances surrounding his death remain unclear, with some arguing he committed suicide and others claiming he was victim of political assassination after uncovering existence of arms trafficking network between Chadian border town of Amdjarass and Sudan involving senior army officers and intelligence service members. Mouanodji in days prior to his death reportedly informed relatives that he was being followed by security services. Abéché attorney general 3 Aug said Mouanodji had killed himself, ruled out investigation into his death. Competition for access to resources continued to fuel violent conflict. Farmer-herder violence 23 Aug left one dead and forced residents to flee in Béssao canton, Logone Oriental province (south). Deadly clashes 28 Aug broke out between Arab nomads and members of sedentary community after dispute over access to water well in Woli (Kanem region in west), with at least four dead. Security forces reportedly detained son of Boko Haram founder. Media 18 Aug reported Chadian security services arrested six suspected Islamic State West Africa Province jihadists, including Muslim Mohammed Yusuf, youngest son of Boko Haram founder.

Political tensions continued to mount ahead of the October presidential election, triggering localised outbreaks of violence and protests; meanwhile, a border attack by suspected Burkinabè army auxiliaries left several dead. Tensions continued to rise ahead of October vote, leading to violent incidents. Political stalemate between President Ouattara – who late July announced fourth term bid – and frustrated opponents continued to exacerbate tensions on ground. Armed individuals 1 Aug burned bus and attacked police vehicle in Abidjan neighbourhood of Yopougon, traditional stronghold of former President Gbagbo, who has been excluded from presidential race. Authorities 11 Aug charged 11 members of Gbagbo’s African People’s Party-Côte d’Ivoire (PPA-CI) with “terrorist acts” and “conspiracy against state authority” for their alleged involvement in incident; PPA-CI denied responsibility, denounced “judicial and political harassment”. Earlier, thousands 9 Aug peacefully demonstrated in Yopougon in support of “common front” between main opposition Democratic Party of Côte d’Ivoire (PDCI) and PPA-CI, demanding reintegration of their leaders on electoral list. Rifts widened within main opposition party. Dissident group within PDCI – whose leader Tidjane Thiam was barred from running in Oct presidential election following court ruling – 18 Aug called on party to nominate replacement candidate. PDCI member and former Commerce Minister Jean-Louis Billon next day announced presidential candidacy under banner of Congrès démocratique (CODE), newly created coalition of 18 smaller opposition parties. Burkinabè militia blamed for several incidents at border. Media reported Burkinabè army auxiliaries (VDPs) 24 Aug detained six Ivorian govt officials on mission in Tougbo subprefecture (Bounkani region in north east) and allegedly transferred them to Burkinabè capital Ouagadougou. Army said unidentified armed men 25 Aug killed four people in assault on Difita village (also Bounkani region); media blamed attack on VDPs (see Burkina Faso).

The peace process between Kinshasa and the Rwanda-backed M23 rebels stalled as fighting continued in the Kivu provinces; other armed group attacks persisted in North Kivu and Ituri provinces, and President Tshisekedi announced a limited cabinet reshuffle. Doha peace process stalled as deadlines passed amid renewed fighting . Implementation of 19 July Doha Declaration of Principles between Kinshasa and Rwanda-backed M23/Congo River Alliance (AFC) rebels faltered as 8 and 18 Aug deadlines for formal talks and final peace deal were missed. Talks around 26 Aug resumed in Qatar, focusing on ceasefire implementation and prisoner exchange. Meanwhile, clashes between govt and M23 rebels continued, also involving their respective allies. In North Kivu province, M23 early Aug occupied new areas in Walikale territory, moving closer to Pinga town. In South Kivu province, fighting around 7 Aug took place notably in Mikenge locality in Fizi territory, and govt and allied Wazalendo militias 27 Aug reportedly recaptured Rugezi village (also Fizi) after intense fighting. Clashes 17-20 Aug killed at least nine people in Kizuka and Muhusi villages, Mwenga territory, causing panic in nearby Uvira town. Fighting also reported around 26 Aug between govt forces and Wazalendo around Uvira. Meanwhile, M23 and Rwanda faced mounting international condemnation over massacres of civilians (see Rwanda). ADF and other armed groups killed scores in North Kivu and Ituri provinces . Notably, Islamic State-affiliated Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) 13-14 Aug killed over 40 civilians in Bapere groupement, North Kivu’s Lubero territory. Ethnic Lendu CODECO militia, ethnic Hema Zaïre militia and allied Thomas Lubanga’s Convention pour la Révolution Populaire (CRP) also continued attacks in both North Kivu and Ituri. President Tshisekedi unveiled minimal govt reshuffle . Tshisekedi 8 Aug reduced cabinet from 54 to 53 members, retaining key figures including PM Judith Suminwa Tuluka, Interior Minister Jacquemain Shabani and FM Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner. Reshuffle failed to bring in key opposition figures but former PM Adolphe Muzito joined as budget minister, ex-civil society activist Floribert Anzuluni as regional integration minister and former UN human rights chief Guillaume Ngefa-Atondoko as justice minister. Meanwhile, military prosecutor 22 Aug demanded death penalty against former President Kabila for alleged war crimes, treason and organising insurrection.

Relations with Addis Ababa remained tense amid Asmara’s deepening engagement with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Ethiopia’s ruling Prosperity Party 8 Aug issued statement accusing “historic enemies” – seen as implicit reference to Eritrea – of seeking to derail country’s progress and return to conflict; comments came after Ethiopian PM Abiy Ahmed late July accused Asmara of pitting Ethiopians against each other, notably through its support of TPLF. Abiy early Aug also reportedly held closed-door meeting, where he told diplomats that Ethiopia was at war and that their diplomatic work should be calibrated accordingly. Information Ministry 27 Aug denied it was working to “stifle Ethiopia’s growth” and insisted on Asmara’s commitment to regional stability. Meanwhile, border communities from Eritrea and Ethiopia’s Tigray region early Aug staged meet-up in Badme town – area long-disputed between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Improvements in relationships among border communities seen as taking place with tacit approval of political leaders in Asmara and Mekelle but not official involvement.

Tigray region witnessed more political turbulence, Addis Ababa’s relations with Asmara remained tense, and security forces struggled to contain the insurgencies plaguing Amhara and Oromia regions. Tigray region remained volatile. Fears of renewed conflict in Tigray persisted amid tensions between federal authorities and Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) led by Debretsion Gebremichael, which is allegedly backed by Asmara (see Eritrea). Intra-Tigrayan political fragmentation exacerbated volatile situation. Notably, Tigray Defence Forces (TDF) 18 Aug attempted to arrest Halefom Mehari, head of district militia office in Mehoni town, Southern Tigray Zone – part of TPLF’s attempt to remove officials appointed under former Interim Regional Administration President Getachew Reda. TDF reportedly shot at demonstrators protesting move, injuring at least five. Incident reinforced concerns that TPLF is tightening its grip on power, though protests suggested resistance to its authority remains strong in Southern Tigray. Zinabu Gebremedhin 26 Aug replaced Haftu Kiros as head of Southern Tigray, triggering protests 29 Aug. Meanwhile, Lt. Gen. Tsadkan, former deputy president under Getachew, 1 Aug announced that several opposition parties, including Getachew’s new Semret party, had formed coalition to challenge TPLF. Tensions with Eritrea ran high. Ruling Prosperity Party 8 Aug accused “historic enemies” – seen as implicit reference to Eritrea – of seeking to derail Ethiopia’s progress and return to conflict. PM Abiy Ahmed early Aug held separate closed-door meeting, where he told diplomats that country was at war (see Eritrea). Clashes continued in Amhara amid federal counter-insurgency operations. Federal forces continued their counter-insurgency campaign in Amhara but failed to yield decisive results against resilient Fano militias. Meanwhile, Fano groups 25 Aug launched new operation dubbed ‘Operation Martyrs’ in at least 18 districts in various zones of Gojjam. Insurgent-govt fighting escalated in Oromia. Clashes between military and Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) intensified, marking first significant escalation in Oromia since Dec 2024 peace deal between OLA splinter group led by Sagni Negasa and regional authorities. OLA 5 Aug staged prison break in Gida Ayana town, East Wollega Zone, freeing over 150 inmates including OLA members. OLA also conducted more abductions, particularly in North Shewa Zone, with over 100 civilians abducted late July-early Aug.

Insecurity continued to mount in the Borgou region near the Nigerian border, while jihadist violence remained low in the north. New security incident reported in Borgou department, located south of country’s conflict hotspots and closer to Nigerian border, after attack on military position in June. Unidentified extremist group 10 Sept targeted police post and health centre in Kalalé town, kidnapping several civilians before govt forces rebuffed assailants, killing three. Authorities 16 Sept also secured release of five hostages taken several months ago in Dangazi village, 10km from Kalalé, following secret negotiations. Meanwhile in north, army 6 Sept reported killing six suspected al-Qaeda-affiliated Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims militants in counter-insurgency operations in Pendjari and W national parks.

Jihadists repeatedly attacked members of the security forces while infighting between rival militant groups left dozens dead; the authorities repressed critical voices amid growing public discontent. Violence remained widespread, as intra-jihadist clashes surged. Al-Qaeda-affiliated Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM) continued frequent attacks on military and army auxiliaries (VDPs), particularly in North, Boucle du Mouhoun, Sahel, Centre-North, Centre-East and East regions, maintaining pressure on major secondary cities. In notable large-scale attacks, JNIM 13 Sept overran Gomboro military camp (Boucle du Mouhoun), killing at least 15 soldiers, and 17 Sept temporarily took control of three military positions in Djibo town (Sahel), killing at least eight. Reports emerged of desertions among army, police and VDPs, particularly in parts of Centre-North, Centre-East and Boucle du Mouhoun. Meanwhile, conflict between JNIM and Islamic State Sahel Province (IS-Sahel) escalated amid latter’s heightened activity; IS-Sahel 16 Sept reportedly killed at least 60 JNIM members near Sebba town (Sahel), with further clashes reported in East region. Govt cracked down on dissent amid mounting discontent among public and security forces. Prosecutors 6 Sept opened treason investigation against Ini Benjamine Doli, lawyer and vocal regime critic, arrested late Aug in capital Ouagadougou. Police mid-Sept arrested VDP from North region following media interview in which he denounced what he said were govt lies about security situation. Suspected Burkinabè agents 13 Sept kidnapped former Burkinabè MP in Ghana, fuelling concerns among Burkinabè political dissidents living there. Meanwhile, in Sahel province, residents of Sebba and Solhan towns 20 Sept protested lack of food and warned of famine. Although authorities 15-18 Sept released journalists Alain Traoré and Adama Bayala, who had been abducted in June-July 2024 and forcibly enrolled as VDPs, at least one other journalist believed to still be at frontlines. In other important developments. Members of Alliance of Sahel States – Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger – 22 Sept withdrew from International Criminal Court, accusing body of being “instrument of neo-colonial repression” and “example of selective justice”. President Capt. Traoré 16 Sept hosted current ECOWAS chief, Sierra Leone President Bio.

The authorities maintained a tight grip in the wake of the elections; Burundi’s military deployment in eastern DR Congo (DRC) suffered further casualties amid clashes with the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group. Repression continued amid UN alarm over election-related crackdown. Amid drift toward one-party rule following legislative and local elections held since June, authorities remained intolerant of dissent. Govt 5 Sept ordered head of Belgian development agency in Burundi to leave country after he shared social media post on fuel shortages. SOS Médias Burundi 16 Sept reported intelligence services late Aug detained social media activist Dieudonné Niyukuri, who recently released videos critical of govt, and four other people. UN experts including rapporteur on human rights for Burundi, Fortuné Gaetan Zongo, 1 Sept expressed concern about increase in “serious human rights violations” during election period, including extrajudicial killings and enforced disappearances; Zongo 19 Sept reiterated concerns at annual UN human rights summit in Geneva city (Switzerland), saying 2025 polls marked by “climate of intimidation” and “weakening and near elimination” of opposition parties, and calling for inclusive dialogue and free elections in 2027. Military continued to fight M23 rebels in neighbouring DRC. Burundian soldiers continued bolstering Congolese forces in their fight against M23 rebels and aligned groups in DRC’s South Kivu province (see DR Congo), with frequent military convoys reported from late Aug onward near border crossings. At least 20 Burundian soldiers killed in Sept, most notably in heavy fighting 10 Sept in province’s Hauts-Plateaux. Meanwhile, security services reportedly continued to target Congolese nationals in Burundi, notably detaining some 500 in Bujumbura Province 8-9 Sept before attempting to return them to DRC. Authorities from 21 Sept onward reportedly evicted some 100 farming families in western Cibitoke commune on allegations of collusion with M23. In another important international development. Regional body Economic Community of Central African States 7 Sept announced former Burundian FM Ézéchiel Nibigira as new head.

Anglophone separatists imposed a lockdown to disrupt the 12 October presidential election, threatening further violence around polling day; unrest could also erupt over the election results amid widespread discontent with President Biya’s decades-long rule and the opposition’s continued lack of unity. Separatist lockdown crippled Anglophone regions. Anglophone separatists 8 Sept imposed lockdown across Anglophone North West and South West regions, shutting schools, businesses and roads to block campaigning for presidential election set for 12 Oct, and prompting thousands to flee to Francophone areas. Rebels threatened further violence during election week and continued attacks on govt forces, notably in South West’s Fako division, with at least nine soldiers and one gendarme killed 5-12 Sept. In North West, separatist militias in Sept allegedly killed up to six civilians in and around regional capital Bamenda while enforcing lockdown, and carried out several ambushes in Boyo, Momo and Bui divisions. Biya’s allies campaigned in his absence. Since announcing candidacy on social media in July, Biya has made no statement on election. In his absence, PM Dion Ngute 12, 17 Sept campaigned in Anglophone regions, while other ministers in Sept campaigned in Far North region, where ruling party fears losing ground to former Biya ministers turned presidential hopefuls Issa Tchiroma and Bello Bouba. Biya 21 Sept-1 Oct travelled to Switzerland reportedly for private reasons. Opposition failed to rally behind single candidate. Union for Change 2025 – coalition of 53 civil society groups and political parties – 13 Sept named Tchiroma as its presidential candidate. Critics questioned Tchiroma’s selection, citing his record defending govt abuses in Anglophone and Far North regions though he enjoys public support. Key opposition figure Maurice Kamto (who has been barred from running) 17 Sept called on 11 opposition candidates to rally behind single contender. Soon after 27 Sept campaign launch, candidates Ateki Caxton and Akere Muna dropped from race to back Bouba. Insecurity persisted in Far North. Boko Haram 6-7 Sept killed at least four in villages of Mayo-Tsanaga division, while security forces 15, 18 Sept repelled Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) attacks near Fotokol town, Logone-et-Chari division. Spate of abductions continued in Sept, with Boko Haram kidnapping about 20 across Far North.

The opposition appeared increasingly divided over whether to participate in the December presidential election, while rebel and criminal violence persisted. Main opposition leader began positioning himself for presidential bid. Bangui 2 Sept launched long-awaited political dialogue with opposition coalition Republican Bloc for the Defence of the Constitution, but coalition spokesperson Martin Ziguélé 22 Sept accused govt of playing “double game” by pressing ahead with preparations for December presidential election without addressing opposition’s demands, including reform of electoral authority and revision of voter roll. Meanwhile, former PM and president of Union for Central African Renewal party Georges-Anicet Dologuélé 2 Sept told media he had renounced his French nationality in late Aug. Move appears to be first step toward running in Dec presidential polls, as 2023 constitution bars dual nationals from holding presidency, and represents tacit acknowledgement of 2023 constitution. Rebel activity and banditry continued to fuel insecurity. Despite signs of decline in rebel operations, armed groups – including Return, Reclamation and Reintegration (3R) and Unity for Peace in the Central African Republic (UPC), which signed April ceasefire agreement with govt – continued to pose security threat. Fighting 2 Sept broke out at mining site in Nana-Bakassa town (Ouham prefecture), leaving 11 people dead and four injured; local sources reported that fighters from 3R and Patriotic Movement for Central Africa (MPC) were involved, highlighting ongoing armed group competition over control of mining sites. Meanwhile, criminal violence remained major security concern. Notably, eco-guards from Wildlife Conservation Society and unidentified gunmen 3 Sept exchanged fire following robbery incident near N’Délé town (Bamingui-Bangoran prefecture). Govt secured symbolic victory with regional bloc’s return to CAR. Bangui 9-10 Sept hosted 16th Heads of State Conference of Economic and Monetary Community of Central Africa (CEMAC) for first time in 15 years; summit also marked return of CEMAC’s headquarters to Bangui, following relocation to Malabo (Equatorial Guinea) during 2013 civil war – a tacit endorsement of govt’s narrative of return to stability.

Authorities initiated a constitutional reform process set to expand the powers of President Déby, a draft pastoral code fuelled tensions between the government and the Catholic Church, and several self-defence groups in the Tibesti region joined a peace agreement with N’Djamena. Déby took further steps to consolidate power. National Assembly 15 Sept overwhelmingly adopted constitutional amendments extending presidential mandate from five to seven years and removing term limits; text moved to Senate for final vote expected in mid-Oct. Draft pastoral code triggered controversy. Catholic bishops from southern Moyen-Chari, Mandoul, Logone Oriental and Logone Occidental provinces declined govt’s invitation to 1-2 Sept workshop on draft pastoral code in Sarh town (Moyen-Chari). Bishops warned that text would exacerbate conflicts as southern communities, where agriculture prevails, view it as favouring herders from northern provinces. Govt proceeded with workshop, however, saying aim was to collect input and draft more balanced code. Eight Christian associations, mostly Catholic, 11 Sept sent open letter to President Déby, denouncing draft pastoral code and partial management of agropastoral conflicts; statement demanded audit of religious representation in public administration, reflecting growing tension between Catholic Church and govt. Meanwhile, herder-farmer conflicts continued in south, with two incidents 1-2 Sept leaving four injured in Logone Oriental province. Amid renewed tensions in gold-rich region, govt signed peace deal with self-defence groups. Army from 9 Sept onward conducted exercises around Miski town in northern Tiberti region in possible intimidation attempt after several local officials criticised provisions of April 2025 peace agreement with Miski Self-Defence Committee militia concerning distribution of region’s gold wealth and granting of mining permits to foreign companies. Déby 16 Sept also dismissed Lt. Gen. Mahamat Abali Salah after latter denounced plundering of Tibesti’s resources, and following day revoked Chadian nationality of two activists who had accused Déby of exploiting gold resources in north for personal gain. Amid renewed tensions in gold-rich region, authorities around 23 Sept announced Diffa Al Watan Popular Committee of Miski, Movement for Alternation and Democracy in Chad (MADAT) and Yorogueï Defense Committee had joined April peace agreement.

The country geared up for the presidential election scheduled for 25 October, with President Ouattara seeking a fourth term and two prominent opposition figures formally excluded; Ouagadougou once again accused Côte d’Ivoire of pursuing destabilisation efforts. Authorities released final list of presidential candidates. Constitutional Council 8 Sept said it had validated only five of 60 applications submitted for upcoming presidential vote. President Ouattara will face four opponents who lack financial and logistical support of two main opposition parties, including Simone Ehivet Gbagbo of Movement of Capable Generations, small party with limited national reach; former minister Jean-Louis Billon running under banner of Congrès démocratique coalition of 18 small opposition parties; former minister Ahoua Don Mello, standing as independent after former President Laurent Gbagbo’s Parti des Peuples Africains (PPA-CI) refused to endorse him; and former minister Henriette Lagou Adjoua, who won less than 1% of votes in 2015 election. Two opposition heavyweights – Laurent Gbagbo and main opposition Democratic Party of Côte d’Ivoire (PDCI)’s Tidjane Thiam – definitively excluded from race . Authorities stepped up repression amid fears of opposition protests. PPA-CI 16 Sept claimed that around 30 members, including former minister Moïse Lida Kouassi, had been arrested since protests held in Aug against exclusion of opposition leaders from election; govt 17 Sept said 18 had since been released. PPA-CI 30 Sept said two other senior members had been charged and imprisoned same day for allegedly “inciting insurrection”. Tensions with Ouagadougou remained high. Burkinabè President Capt. Traoré 28 Sept for first time confirmed late Aug arrest of six Ivorian govt officials near shared border; Traoré said officials were engaged in acts of “espionage”, and once again accused Côte d’Ivoire of serving as rear base for “enemies of Burkina Faso” and govt of “flirting with terrorists”.

A military court sentenced former President Kabila to death for allegedly collaborating with Rwanda-backed M23 rebels; the conviction is likely to undermine the Doha peace process between Kinshasa and the M23. Conviction of former president ratcheted up tensions with M23 rebels. Military Court in Kinshasa 30 Sept sentenced Kabila to death in absentia for war crimes and treason on accusations of collaborating with M23 rebellion in eastern provinces. M23 immediately criticised conviction as “serious violation of the declaration of principles” signed in July by Kinshasa and M23 representatives in Qatar. Development could jeopardise fragile Doha peace process as rebel group may escalate demands or withdraw from negotiations in response. Ceasefire implementation and M23 withdrawal remained elusive in east. In North Kivu province, M23 7 Sept recaptured Shoa town in Masisi territory, while army early Sept made tactical gains in Walikale territory. Air force later in month launched airstrikes on rebel positions in both Masisi and Walikale, notably destroying Mpeti bridge leading to strategic site of Pinga on 28 Sept (Walikale). In South Kivu province, govt troops, allied Wazalendo armed groups and Burundian forces in Sept clashed with M23 in Mwenga territory, and rebels 21 Sept seized Nzibira mining town in Walungu territory. Rift widened between Kinshasa and Wazalendo. After army late Aug clashed with Wazalendo units in Uvira territory (South Kivu), confrontation intensified over appointment as deputy defence commander for South Kivu of Gen. Olivier Gasita – whom Wazalendo and locals accuse of collaborating with M23; military 8 Sept reportedly opened fire on protesters demanding Gasita’s departure in Uvira city, leaving several dead. General was exfiltrated following night to Burundi and then returned to Kinshasa, but situation remained tense between army and Wazalendo. Also, clashes among Wazalendo factions from 17 Sept onward killed at least eight, including three civilians in Mwenga town, South Kivu. ADF continued to escalate attacks on civilians in eastern provinces. In North Kivu, Islamic State-affiliated Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) overnight 8-9 Sept killed 72 people at funeral in Ntoyo village (Lubero territory) and 26 Sept killed at least eight people on Oïcha-Mamove axis (Beni territory) as group advanced further into new areas.

Asmara condemned Ethiopia’s Red Sea ambitions in response to Addis Ababa’s progressively more pointed targeting of the port of Assab, while top U.S. and Eritrean officials met in New York city. Tensions ran high between Eritrea and Ethiopia over latter’s sea access ambitions. Information Minister Yemane Gebre Meskel 15 Sept denounced Ethiopia’s “reckless sabre-rattling” after several Ethiopian govt officials became more assertive in their quest for sea access. Notably, Ethiopia’s PM Abiy Ahmed 1 Sept stated that surrendering access to Red Sea was “mistake… [that can be] resolved tomorrow” and Ethiopian defence ministry official, Maj. Gen. Teshome Gemechu, late Aug set out argument for why Ethiopia might seek to acquire Eritrean port of Assab, framing it as matter of “national survival”. Meanwhile, c redible reports early Sept emerged that Abiy has set up “Command Centre” to coordinate military and intelligence operations related to Eritrea. Washington and Asmara held high-level talks in New York. U.S. Senior Advisor for Africa, Massad Boulos, 24 Sept met with FM Osman Saleh on sidelines of UN General Assembly, with Boulos noting “desire on both sides to re-establish a productive bilateral relationship”. Earlier, Boulos 17 Sept held talks with Abiy in Ethiopia. Engagement continued between Eritrean and Tigrayan communities. Tigray People’s Liberation Front chairperson Debretsion Gebremichel and Tigray Interim Regional Administration President Tadesse Werede early Sept made carefully framed comments in support of engagement between Eritrean and Tigrayan communities living along shared border, rather than between Tigray and Eritrea.

Tensions between the federal government, Tigray Interim Regional Administration (TIRA) and Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) ran high, the Fano insurgency launched a new and bloody offensive in Amhara, and relations with Eritrea remained fraught. Tensions continued to build in Tigray region. Protests against TIRA’s moves to replace Southern Tigray Zone leadership (appointed under ousted TIRA President Getachew Reda) with individuals aligned with TPLF late Aug-early Sept led to violent incidents, including grenade attack in Maichew town. Former Southern Tigray head Haftu Kiros, who was sacked late Aug, reportedly joined Tigray Peace Force – split-off from Tigray security forces. Meanwhile , TIRA President Lt. Gen. Tadesse Werede 8-9 Sept warned of “cloud of war” in Tigray, pointing to federal govt’s “failure to honour” 2022 Pretoria Peace Agreement as root cause of region’s vulnerability; Werede 11 Sept also rejected National Election Board’s May revocation of TPLF’s legal status as “unacceptable” and called for political settlement. Fano militias escalated offensive in Amhara. Fragmented Amhara nationalist militant groups known as Fano from 24 Sept onward significantly escalated operations in Amhara region’s North and South Wollo zones, and to lesser extent in Gojjam zone. In Wollo, Fano units inflicted heavy casualties on federal forces, notably on outskirts of Weldiya town, and temporarily seized control of key locations such as Mekane Selam town (connecting Gojjam and Wollo). Govt 27-28 Sept conducted retaliatory drone strikes in Wollo, but fighting continued. Fano also launched deadly attacks in Oromia region. Notably, news early Sept emerged that suspected Fano gunmen 29 Aug stormed Hoomaa Gaalessaa village in Horro Guduru Wollega Zone, killing at least 25 civilians and displacing thousands. Sporadic clashes persisted in Oromia. After Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) late July launched first significant offensive since Dec 2024, fighting between OLA insurgents and federal forces declined. Amid sporadic clashes, skirmish around 12 Sept reportedly resulted in death of senior police commander Getachew Bezu. In other important developments. Govt doubled down on quest for sea access, further ratcheting up tensions with Asmara (see Eritrea). PM Abiy 9 Sept inaugurated Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam despite downstream countries’ water security concerns (see Egypt, Nile Waters).
